practice_questions.text: State one type of offering made during Buddhist puja.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: flowers / candles or lamps / incense / food / water / fruit. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by Samatha meditation.
practice_questions.marks: Samatha is a calming form of meditation [1] that focuses attention on a single object such as the breath [1] in order to still the mind and develop tranquillity / prepare for deeper states of absorption [1]. (Any two of these points.) [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of pilgrimage to Bodh Gaya for Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Bodh Gaya is the site of the Buddha's enlightenment under the Bodhi tree [1]; pilgrims travel there to meditate, make offerings and circumambulate the Mahabodhi Temple [1]; visiting can deepen faith and motivate personal practice by connecting the pilgrim to the Buddha's own experience [1]. (3 separate developed points required.) [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which meditation is important for Buddhists.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Vipassana meditation develops insight into the Three Marks of Existence (anicca, dukkha, anatta) — the Dhammapada 273–276 teaches that the Noble Eightfold Path is the supreme path, and Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration are key elements of it. This shows meditation is essential to ending suffering.
• Samatha meditation calms the mind, allowing practitioners to enter deeper states of concentration (jhana) that reduce the influence of greed, hatred and ignorance — the three poisons that perpetuate rebirth.
• Metta bhavana (loving-kindness) extends goodwill to all beings, cultivating the compassion taught in the Karaniya Metta Sutta and reducing aversion.
[6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 simple point, 2 developed, 3 with teaching/source]

practice_questions.text: 'Meditation is the most important Buddhist practice.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Meditation (samadhi) is one of the three strands of the Noble Eightfold Path and directly addresses the mind — the root of both suffering and liberation. The Dhammapada 273–276 presents the Eightfold Path, which includes Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration, as the supreme way to end suffering.
• Without meditation, insight into the Three Marks of Existence cannot arise, so liberation from samsara is impossible.
• The Buddha himself attained enlightenment through meditation at Bodh Gaya, making it the foundational practice.

Arguments against:
• Puja and devotional practice cultivate merit (punna) and the right mental attitude, and for many lay Buddhists who cannot pursue intensive meditation, devotion is the primary form of practice. The Dhammapada 183 presents moral conduct and mental purification together, not meditation alone.
• Ethics (sila) is listed in the Threefold Way before meditation (samadhi) — without moral conduct, meditation cannot develop correctly. Keeping the Five Precepts is arguably as foundational.
• In Mahayana Buddhism, the Bodhisattva vow to save all beings places compassionate action alongside meditation as equally important.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named Buddhist teachings, clear contrast between traditions (Theravada vs Mahayana), explicit weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with some teaching reference; conclusion offered.
Developing: One side stronger than the other; some Buddhist content; limited or no teaching references.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no Buddhist teaching. [15 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of mudras (hand positions) in Buddhist worship.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: mudras are symbolic hand gestures depicted on Buddha images [1]; each mudra carries a specific meaning — for example, the earth-touching mudra recalls the moment of enlightenment and the teaching mudra recalls the first sermon [1]; they remind worshippers of key events in the Buddha's life and the qualities they are cultivating [1]. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'Shahadah'.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for: the Islamic declaration of faith / the statement 'There is no god but Allah and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah' / la ilaha illa-llah, muhammadur-rasulu-llah. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims do when they perform wudu.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for any two of the following points: washing the face / washing the hands and arms to the elbow / wiping the head / washing the feet / it is ritual purification performed before Salah / the purpose is physical and spiritual cleanliness before standing before Allah. [2 marks — 1 mark per valid point]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between Salah and du'a in Islamic worship.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for: Salah is formal / structured / has a set number of units (raka't) / uses Arabic / performed at five set times / requires wudu and facing the qibla (any two developed). Du'a is personal / informal / can be in any language / at any time / in any posture / is supplication from the heart (any one developed). Award three marks for a clear, developed contrast covering both forms. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the Five Pillars are important for Sunni Muslims.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Five Pillars unite all Sunni Muslims in shared practice regardless of nationality or culture — performing the same prayers at the same times creates a global community (ummah). Surah 2:238 commands Muslims to maintain prayers carefully, showing these are divine obligations.
• The Five Pillars structure daily life around submission to Allah, reinforcing Tawhid — the belief in Allah's absolute oneness. Each pillar is an act of obedience that strengthens faith and reminds Muslims of their purpose.
• Salat, performed five times daily, provides regular direct communication with Allah, preventing the believer from becoming spiritually distant.
• The Pillars are described using the analogy of a house and its pillars — without them, a Muslim's faith has no structural support.
Mastering: Two developed points each supported by a named source of wisdom, clear explanation of significance, and coherent expression.
Secure: Two developed points with at least one source of wisdom.
Developing: Two points but limited development or no source.
Emerging: One point, brief or undeveloped. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The Five Pillars are the most important feature of Muslim life.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Five Pillars are obligatory for all Sunni Muslims and cover the full scope of worship — declaration, prayer, giving, fasting and pilgrimage. They are the structural framework ('the pillars of the house') without which faith collapses.
• Salat, five times daily, is the most regular reminder of Allah's presence and keeps Muslims in constant communication with God. Surah 2:238 stresses maintaining prayer with care.
• The Shahadah is the gateway to Islam and encapsulates the core theological belief in Tawhid and the prophethood of Muhammad.
• Without the Pillars being fulfilled, a Muslim cannot be said to be fully practising their faith.

Arguments against / other perspectives:
• Shi'a Muslims follow the Ten Obligatory Acts, which extend beyond the Five Pillars to include Khums, Amr-bil-Maroof, Nahi Anil Munkar, Tawalla and Tabarra. For them, the Five Pillars alone do not cover the full requirement.
• Inner faith and correct belief (niyyah, Tawhid) could be argued to be more fundamental than external ritual practice — without sincere intention, the actions carry no spiritual weight.
• Other features of Muslim life such as the Qur'an, the Sunnah of the Prophet and adherence to Shari'ah law shape moral conduct as much as the Pillars do.
• Du'a — personal, spontaneous prayer — represents the most direct and intimate form of communication with Allah and is practised beyond the structured Pillars.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (e.g. Surah 2:238, Surah 2:186), explicit comparison of Sunni and Shi'a practice, explicit weighing, and a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed, at least one source, clear conclusion.
Developing: Some engagement with both sides but limited sources or thin conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief response with minimal development. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Ten Obligatory Acts observed by Shi'a Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for a clear, accurate outline identifying at least five of the Ten Obligatory Acts with brief explanation: Salat (prayer), Sawm (fasting), Zakat (almsgiving), Khums (20% tax on earnings), Hajj (pilgrimage), Jihad (striving in the way of Allah), Amr-bil-Maroof (commanding good), Nahi Anil Munkar (forbidding wrong), Tawalla (love for the friends of Allah), Tabarra (disassociation from enemies of Allah). Award three marks for a developed, accurate outline covering distinct acts. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what the term 'atman' means in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: The eternal self or soul present within every living being. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Hindus mean by 'samsara'.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: the continuous cycle of birth, death and rebirth; the atman is reborn into a new body after death; the form of rebirth is determined by karma; the cycle continues until the atman achieves moksha/liberation. [2 marks — 1 for a simple statement, 2 for a developed description]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Hindu teaching about karma as a form of cosmic justice.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: karma means 'action' and refers to the moral law of cause and effect; every action generates consequences across lifetimes; good actions produce positive karma, harmful actions produce negative karma; it is not punishment from a deity but an impersonal law; the Bhagavad Gita (III 3-9) teaches that all beings must act and should do so rightly; parabdha karma is already bearing fruit while kriyamana karma is being created by present choices. [3 marks — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a well-outlined account with specific detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain two different Hindu understandings of the relationship between atman and Brahman.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Advaita Vedanta (Shankara): atman and Brahman are identical; there is ultimately one reality; the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (III 7 15-23) describes Brahman as the inner controller; liberation means realising this identity.
• Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja): atman is real and distinct from Brahman but part of Brahman's being; liberation means loving union with a personal God rather than complete merger.
• The distinction matters practically: Advaita aims at loss of separate self; Vaishnava traditions aim at eternal relationship with God.
[6 marks — 3 marks per understanding: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a well-explained account with specific detail or source]

practice_questions.text: 'The concept of maya makes it impossible for Hindus to live meaningfully in the material world.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments that could support the statement: if the material world is maya (illusion), attachments and goals in it may seem pointless; Advaita teaching that only Brahman is ultimately real could lead to withdrawal from social and moral responsibility; some ascetics do renounce worldly life entirely as a response to maya.

Arguments that could challenge the statement: maya does not mean the world is unreal, only that it is not the ultimate reality; detachment (as taught in Bhagavad Gita II 11-13) means acting without clinging to results, not refusing to act; nishkam karma teaches engaged, dutiful action in the world without self-seeking; jivan mukti shows liberation is compatible with remaining in the world; many Hindus live very actively in society guided by dharma, artha and kama alongside moksha.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita II 11-13, III 3-9; Shankara vs Ramanuja debate), explicit weighing of the arguments, and a justified conclusion explaining why the statement is an oversimplification.
Secure: two clear perspectives with some use of Hindu teaching, conclusion present.
Developing: one side more developed than the other; some relevant content; limited use of sources.
Emerging: one-sided or very brief; little specific Hindu content.

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between sakam karma and nishkam karma.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: sakam karma is action performed with a desired result in mind; the person seeks personal gain, reward or recognition; such action binds the atman more firmly to samsara; nishkam karma is desireless action performed without attachment to the outcome; it is taught in the Bhagavad Gita (III 3-9) as the highest form of action; nishkam karma leads towards liberation while sakam karma increases bondage. [3 marks — 1 for naming the distinction, 2 for describing one type, 3 for a full account of both with the implication for rebirth/liberation]

practice_questions.text: State what Christians mean when they describe God as omnipotent.
practice_questions.marks: God is all-powerful / God can do anything / God has unlimited power. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Christians believe about God as both transcendent and immanent.
practice_questions.marks: Transcendent: God is beyond the created world, above and outside human experience. [1 mark] Immanent: God is present within the world and personally involved with human beings. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Christian belief in the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks from: the belief that one God exists as three persons [1]; named as Father, Son and Holy Spirit [1]; the persons are distinct but united in one divine being [1]; expressed in the Nicene Creed or Apostles' Creed [1].

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why belief in the Trinity is important for Christians.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- The Trinity shapes Christian worship and baptism, which is carried out in the name of all three persons. John 14:16-17 shows Jesus promising the Spirit as advocate, grounding Trinitarian belief in scripture. [up to 3 marks]
- The Trinity means God is eternally relational; because God is three persons in relationship, love is fundamental to his nature. Philippians 2:5-8 shows the Son willingly taking human form, expressing self-giving love within the Godhead. [up to 3 marks]
- Other valid points: the Trinity connects creation (Father), redemption (Son) and sanctification (Spirit); it shapes the Lord's Prayer (addressed to the Father) and the work of the Spirit in Christian lives. [3 marks per point: 1 for a simple statement, 2 for development, 3 for development with a named source]

practice_questions.text: 'Belief in the Trinity is the most important Christian belief about God.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- The Trinity is affirmed in both the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed, making it one of the most formally agreed Christian doctrines across denominations.
- It shapes every act of Christian worship: baptism, prayer, the Gloria and the structure of the Mass are all Trinitarian.
- Philippians 2:5-8 and John 14:16-17 provide biblical grounding for seeing the Son and Spirit as fully divine alongside the Father.
- Without the Trinity, the incarnation and atonement lose their significance: Jesus is only a saviour if he is fully divine.

Arguments against / alternative views:
- Unitarians such as the Christadelphians argue that strict monotheism — God as one person — is more important, and that the Trinity is a later human doctrine not found in scripture.
- Some Christians would argue that God's benevolence (love) is the most fundamental attribute, since without it the other attributes become frightening rather than reassuring.
- God's omnipotence might be seen as more foundational: if God is not all-powerful, then his promises, creation and salvation are all in doubt.
- Immanence may be more practically significant for many believers: the felt presence of God in daily life shapes behaviour and comfort more directly than doctrinal definitions.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Nicene Creed, Philippians 2:5-8, Unitarian position); explicit weighing of which belief is 'most important' with a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with at least one named source; some comparison and a conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger than the other; limited sources; conclusion present but not fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; little or no use of sources; no real conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the Nicene Creed is used in Christian worship.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: said together at Sunday Mass / Anglican Communion service as a statement of shared faith [1]; used at baptisms to express the faith the candidate is entering [1]; used to unite Christians across denominations in affirming core Trinitarian belief [1]. [1 mark per valid point, max 2]

practice_questions.text: State the name given to the Shi'a framework of five foundational beliefs.
practice_questions.marks: Usul ad-Din [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims mean by 'the six articles of faith'.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a response that includes: the six articles are the core beliefs that Sunni Muslims must hold (1 mark); they include belief in Allah, angels, holy books, prophets, the Day of Judgement and predestination/al-Qadr (1 mark for naming at least two correctly, or for a clear description of their function as a framework of belief). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi'a Islam.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of the following correctly named and briefly described: Al-Tawhid (the oneness of Allah); Al-Adl (divine justice); Al-Nubuwwah (prophethood); Al-Imamah (the Imamate or divinely appointed leadership); Al-Ma'ad (resurrection and the Day of Judgement). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Shi'a concept of the Imamate differs from Sunni beliefs about leadership in Islam.
practice_questions.marks: Possible content: Shi'a Muslims believe that after the Prophet Muhammad, leadership passed to a line of twelve divinely appointed Imams descended from the Prophet's family, beginning with Ali; Sunni Muslims do not accept hereditary divine leadership and hold that the community is guided by the consensus of scholars and the Sunnah (1+1 mark for point and development). The twelve Imams in Shi'a belief are considered infallible interpreters of scripture and law; Sunni scholars do not claim infallibility (1+1 mark). The Hadith al-Thaqalayn is cited by Shi'a Muslims to support the special authority of the Prophet's household; Sunni Muslims interpret this hadith differently (1+1 mark). [6 marks: 3 marks per point — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'The differences between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims are more significant than what they share.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Imamate (Al-Imamah) is a uniquely Shi'a belief with no Sunni equivalent — it changes the entire structure of religious authority; Al-Adl (divine justice) as a root of faith is absent from the Sunni framework; historical divisions over leadership after the Prophet led to lasting community separation; different hadith collections and legal schools reflect genuinely divergent traditions. Arguments against: Both traditions hold Tawhid as the most fundamental belief; both accept the prophethood of Muhammad and the authority of the Qur'an; both expect a Day of Judgement and hold similar eschatological beliefs; the Five Pillars are shared in practice; the six articles and five roots overlap significantly in content (Allah, prophethood, afterlife). Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Surah 4:136, Hadith al-Thaqalayn, Surah 74:38), explicit weighing of the significance of shared vs divergent beliefs, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides developed with some reference to sources; conclusion present. Developing: Some argument with basic evidence; one-sided or limited. Emerging: Brief, one-sided, little evidence. [15 marks: 10 AO1 + 5 AO2; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: State one belief that is unique to Shi'a Islam and not found in the Sunni six articles of faith.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: Al-Adl (divine justice) / Al-Imamah (the Imamate / belief in divinely appointed Imams). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one type of prayer used by Christians.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: adoration / confession / thanksgiving / intercessions / supplication / extempore prayer / the Lord's Prayer / chant / meditational prayer. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during a Quaker meeting.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Points may include: there is no set order or minister (1); worshippers sit in silence (1); anyone may speak if moved by the Spirit (1); no music or set prayers are used (1). Maximum 2 marks. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between infant baptism and believers' baptism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per valid difference up to 3. Points may include: infant baptism is for babies / believers' baptism is for those who make a personal confession of faith (1); infant baptism uses sprinkling / believers' baptism uses full immersion (1); parents and godparents make promises in infant baptism / the candidate speaks for themselves in believers' baptism (1); Catholics and Anglicans practise infant baptism / Baptists practise believers' baptism (1). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Eucharist is important for Christians.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks per reason (1 for a basic point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority). Points may include:
• The Eucharist re-enacts the Last Supper — Jesus commanded 'Do this in remembrance of me' (1 Corinthians 11:24), so it is an act of obedience and a way of staying connected to Christ's sacrifice (3).
• For Catholics it makes Christ truly present through transubstantiation — the bread and wine become his body and blood (Matthew 26:26-28) — making every Mass an encounter with the risen Lord (3).
• It builds community — sharing bread and wine together unites believers as the body of Christ, reflecting Paul's teaching that 'we, though many, are one body' (1 Corinthians 10:17) (3).
• For Protestant Christians it is a memorial, a symbol of Christ's saving work, helping them refocus on grace rather than their own efforts (2). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Liturgical worship is the best way for Christians to worship God.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sides with named denominations and scripture references, a clear weighing of arguments, and a well-justified conclusion that goes beyond 'it depends on the person'. E.g. considers traditional arguments for liturgical worship (continuity, theological precision, Matthew 26:26-28 in the Mass) against charismatic/informal arguments (John 4:24 'spirit and truth', Romans 8:14 Spirit-led prayer, Quaker silent waiting). Conclusion explains WHY one view is more compelling with reasoning. [13-15 marks]
Secure: Two developed arguments on each side with some use of Christian teaching; conclusion present but not fully reasoned. [9-12 marks]
Developing: Some relevant points, one side better developed than the other, limited use of scripture or denomination names. [5-8 marks]
Emerging: Brief points with little development or evaluation; limited or no reference to Christian teaching. [1-4 marks]
SPaG assessed on this question.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christians use the Lord's Prayer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks per way. Points may include:
• Used in communal liturgical worship — the Lord's Prayer features in Catholic Mass, Anglican services and most Christian denominations' public worship, providing a shared form of prayer that unites believers across the world (Matthew 6:9-13, Luke 11:1-4) (3).
• Used in private devotion — individual Christians say the Lord's Prayer as part of their daily personal prayer routine, using it as a model that covers all key elements (praise, petition, forgiveness, protection) (3).
• Said at rites of passage — it is commonly used at baptisms, weddings and funerals, marking key Christian life events with the words taught by Jesus (2).
• Used as a teaching tool — children and new Christians learn to pray by memorising the Lord's Prayer, as Jesus intended it as a template for all prayer (Luke 11:1-4) (2). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what the Ner Tamid represents in a synagogue.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: G-d's eternal/constant presence; the menorah that burned in the Temple; the eternal nature of G-d. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the Bimah in a synagogue.
practice_questions.marks: The Bimah is a raised platform in the synagogue [1] from which the Torah is read aloud to the congregation during services [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three features found in a synagogue and their significance.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: the Ark (Aron Kodesh) stores the Torah scrolls and is the focal point of worship; the Ner Tamid is a lamp that burns continuously, symbolising G-d's eternal presence; the Bimah is the raised reading platform where the Torah is chanted; the Sefer Torah is the handwritten Torah scroll, the holiest object in the synagogue; the lack of images reflects the commandment against representing G-d (Exodus 20:4). [3 marks — 1 mark each]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two differences between Orthodox and Reform synagogue worship.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In Orthodox synagogues men and women are separated by a mechitzah (partition), whereas in Reform synagogues they sit together. This reflects differing understandings of the binding nature of traditional law: Orthodox Jews follow halakha strictly, while Reform Jews believe the tradition can develop.
• Orthodox services are conducted entirely in Hebrew, with only men leading prayer. Reform services may use English alongside Hebrew, and women may lead prayers and become rabbis. Deuteronomy 10:12-13 calls all Jews to serve G-d wholeheartedly, but interpretations of how to do so differ.
• In Orthodox communities a minyan requires ten adult men; many Reform congregations count women towards the ten.
[6 marks — 3 marks per difference: 1 for a simple statement, 2 for development, 3 for a relevant source of wisdom]

practice_questions.text: 'The Talmud is more important to Jewish practice than the Tenakh.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Talmud provides the practical guidance on how to apply the Torah in daily life — without its rulings, Jews would not know how to observe Shabbat, keep kosher, or conduct lifecycle ceremonies. The Written Torah often gives only general principles.
• The Talmud has been the living law of diaspora Judaism for almost 2,000 years; Maimonides' legal codes and later authorities all build on Talmudic interpretation.
• For many Orthodox Jews, Talmud study is the highest religious act — the principle that Torah study equals all other commandments shows its practical primacy.

Arguments against:
• The Tenakh is the Written Law given by G-d to Moses at Sinai; the Talmud is a human (rabbinic) interpretation of that law. The Torah itself must logically take precedence.
• The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) and the core commandments all derive from the Tenakh, which is recited and read aloud at every synagogue service. The Sefer Torah is the most sacred object in the building.
• Without the Tenakh there would be nothing for the Talmud to interpret: the Written Law is the root, the Oral Law its branches.
• Some liberal Jewish movements give less authority to Talmudic rulings while still honouring the Tenakh.

Mastering: Both sides are fully developed with named sources (Deuteronomy 6:4, Talmud, Sefer Torah, rabbinic tradition), differences between Orthodox and Reform positions explored, and a justified conclusion that weighs which is more foundational to practice.
Secure: Clear arguments on both sides with relevant named sources and a conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points on both sides but sources limited or underdeveloped; conclusion present but not fully reasoned.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no reference to sources. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Jews believe about the purpose of prayer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: prayer enables communication with G-d; the three daily prayer times (Shacharit, Mincha, Ma'ariv) structure the whole day around G-d; prayer includes praise, confession, thanksgiving and supplication; the Amidah's nineteen blessings address G-d's greatness and human needs; private prayer (e.g. Psalms, Grace after meals) maintains a personal relationship with G-d. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

practice_questions.text: State one purpose of marriage according to Christian teaching.
practice_questions.marks: One of the following: mutual companionship; procreation and upbringing of children; sexual union within a committed relationship; a public covenant before God. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Islamic marriage ceremony (nikah).
practice_questions.marks: Credit any two developed points, for example: the ceremony requires the consent of both parties; witnesses must be present; the mahr (gift from husband to wife) is agreed; an offer (ijab) and acceptance (qubul) are made. [1 mark per point, 2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Outline religious teachings about the purpose of the family.
practice_questions.marks: Credit three developed points drawn from one or more traditions. Examples: Christians see the family as a place where faith is nurtured and love is practised (the Catholic Catechism describes it as the 'domestic church'); Islam sees the family as the cornerstone of the ummah, with parents responsible for passing on faith; non-religious perspectives value the family for human flourishing and wellbeing rather than divine command. [1 mark per point, 3 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two different religious attitudes to contraception.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Credit two well-developed points, each with a supporting teaching or source of authority.
Example points: The Roman Catholic Church (Humanae Vitae, 1968) teaches that artificial contraception is morally impermissible because every sexual act must remain open to new life; the purposes of marriage are both unitive and procreative and cannot be separated. Most Protestant denominations accept artificial contraception, viewing family planning as responsible stewardship and arguing that the purposes of marriage include love and companionship as ends in themselves. Islam generally permits contraception for valid reasons such as spacing births or protecting health, though permanent sterilisation without medical necessity is discouraged. [3 marks per point: 1 for a simple point, 2 for a developed point, 3 for a point developed with a named source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'Religious teachings about marriage are irrelevant in modern society.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (statement is true):
- Cohabitation is now common practice in Britain, suggesting that many people form stable relationships without religious marriage.
- Humanist and non-religious ethics judge relationships by quality (consent, honesty, care) not religious form, making religious definitions seem culturally relative.
- The 2014 legalisation of same-sex marriage shows that civil law has moved beyond traditional religious definitions.
- Many couples who marry in church do so for cultural reasons rather than genuine religious belief.

Arguments against (statement is false):
- Christian teaching on marriage (Matthew 19:4-6; Genesis 2:22-25) continues to shape the values of millions and is upheld by large denominations worldwide.
- Islamic nikah remains central to Muslim family life globally, governing rights, responsibilities and social structures.
- Religious teachings on fidelity, commitment and covenant offer a framework that even secular commentators acknowledge as socially valuable.
- Many people still choose religious ceremonies because they believe marriage gains deeper meaning before God.

Mastering: Both sides argued with developed reasoning; named sources used (e.g. Humanae Vitae, Matthew 19:4-6); explicit weighing of arguments; a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with some development; at least one source referenced; a conclusion reached.
Developing: Some arguments on both sides; limited use of sources; conclusion may be brief or underdeveloped.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; no sources; little or no conclusion. [15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about celibacy.
practice_questions.marks:
Credit two well-developed points with supporting reasoning or sources.
Example points: Catholic teaching holds that celibacy is a special gift, following the example of Jesus and St Paul (1 Corinthians 7:8), and priests and members of religious orders take vows of celibacy to devote themselves fully to God. Protestant teaching generally does not regard celibacy as spiritually superior to marriage: clergy marry freely, and marriage is seen as the expected context for most Christians' lives. [3 marks per point: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a source of wisdom and authority]

before.exam_tip_html: On the 15-mark “Discuss” question, examiners want you to present multiple views with reasons — not just describe one side. On marriage and sexuality, that means: at minimum, a traditional religious view and a progressive or non-religious view, with reasons for each. Always name your religious tradition (Christianity or Islam) and use specific teachings or texts where you can. The command word “Discuss” requires a justified conclusion — you must say which view you find most persuasive and why. SPaG is assessed here, so spell key terms accurately: “fidelity,” “cohabitation,” “celibacy,” “contraception,” “procreation.” For shorter “Explain” questions (6 marks), two well-developed points each supported by a teaching or source of authority will reach the top band.

practice_questions.text: State the constitutional title given to the Monarch in relation to the Church of England.
practice_questions.marks: Supreme Governor of the Church of England. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by secularisation.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that include: the process by which religion loses social significance / influence over public life (1 mark); reference to declining church attendance, changing laws or reduced role of religion in institutions (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the Church of England is part of British public life.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each (up to 3) for any of: bishops in the House of Lords / Lords Spiritual; the Monarch as Supreme Governor of the Church of England; church schools educating roughly a quarter of state primary pupils; public holidays such as Christmas and Easter reflecting the Christian calendar; national services of thanksgiving or mourning held in churches; the Education Act 1988 requiring broadly Christian collective worship in state schools. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which religious and secular values may clash over medical ethics.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Responses may include:
• Euthanasia: many Christians and Muslims oppose assisted dying on the grounds that life is sacred (Exodus 20:13; Psalm 139:13) and only God should determine when life ends. Secular ethicists and Humanists argue that self-determination means individuals should control end-of-life decisions.
• Abortion: religious traditions often teach that life begins at conception, making abortion morally equivalent to taking life. Secular law in Britain permits abortion up to 24 weeks, prioritising the woman’s autonomy.
• Genetic manipulation: religious objectors argue that embryo selection treats human life as raw material, violating human dignity. Humanists tend to support therapeutic gene editing that reduces suffering, provided it is safe and fairly used.
[6 marks — 3 marks per clash: 1 for identifying the issue, 2 for explaining the religious view, 3 for including a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: '‘Britain should be a fully secular state, with no special role for religion in public life.’ Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• In a multi-faith and increasingly non-religious society, privileging one religion (Christianity) in law and Parliament is undemocratic. The 2021 census recorded fewer than half of people identifying as Christian for the first time.
• Humanists UK and the National Secular Society argue that state neutrality on religion protects all citizens equally, whether believers, agnostics or atheists.
• The Education Act 1988 requirement for broadly Christian worship in state schools is outdated in a diverse society; secular collective assemblies would include all pupils equally.
• Equality law requires equal treatment regardless of religion; having bishops in the Lords gives one faith group preferential political access.

Arguments against:
• The Church of England provides social infrastructure (schools, food banks, chaplaincy in hospitals and prisons) that benefits the whole country, not just Christians. Removing its establishment could reduce this contribution.
• The Lords Spiritual bring pastoral and moral perspectives to legislation that purely party-political peers may lack. Many bishops have championed social justice causes.
• Religious freedom includes the freedom of communities to express their values publicly and for religion to have a voice in national debate. A fully secular state could silence legitimate religious perspectives.
• The Christian heritage of Britain has shaped its democratic values, common law and welfare tradition; severing this connection could undermine rather than strengthen shared identity.

Mastering (13–15 marks): Both sides fully developed with specific examples (e.g. Education Act 1988, Humanists UK, bishops in the Lords); sources of wisdom referenced; explicit weighing of arguments; clear, justified conclusion addressing whether a fully secular state is desirable.
Secure (9–12 marks): Both sides explained with some development; at least one specific reference; a conclusion reached.
Developing (5–8 marks): One side more developed than the other; limited specific references; partial conclusion.
Emerging (1–4 marks): Brief, one-sided or largely descriptive; few or no specific references. [15 marks including SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a faith school.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that include: a state-funded school run by or linked to a religious body (1 mark); which may prioritise admissions from its own faith community / teach from a faith perspective / appoint staff on religious grounds (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: State one Christian teaching about the nature of God.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of the following: God is omnipotent / omniscient / omnibenevolent / loving / transcendent / immanent / personal. Accept any accurate statement of a divine attribute supported by the tradition. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what religious believers mean when they say God is omnibenevolent.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks: omnibenevolent means all-good or all-loving (1 mark); this means God acts with perfect goodness and love towards all people at all times, as expressed in 1 John 4:8 (‘God is love’) (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline two religious responses to the problem of evil and suffering.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for each of two responses identified (e.g. the free will defence; suffering as a spiritual test/means of growth; divine solidarity/theology of the cross), plus 1 mark for developing one of them (e.g. without free will humans could not genuinely love God). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which a believer might respond to the challenge that God cannot be good if evil and suffering exist.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per response): 1 mark for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source. Example responses: (1) Free will defence — God gave humans genuine free will so that love and virtue are possible; moral evil is a consequence of human freedom, not of God’s failure; Genesis 1:31 shows God’s creation was originally ‘very good’. (2) Theology of the cross — God entered into human suffering through Jesus Christ; the crucifixion shows divine solidarity; the resurrection promises suffering does not have the final word. (3) Suffering as a call to return — Jeremiah 5:19 frames suffering as a consequence of turning from God and an invitation to renewed relationship. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The existence of evil and suffering proves that God does not exist.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: The logical problem of evil (Mackie) argues that an omnipotent, omnibenevolent God and evil cannot co-exist; if God could prevent suffering and does not, he is either not all-powerful or not all-good. Natural evil — earthquakes, disease — cannot be blamed on human choices, making the free will defence insufficient for this category of suffering. Humanists point out that a universe of random, pointless suffering fits an atheistic worldview far better than a theistic one.

Arguments against: The free will defence: genuine love requires genuine freedom; moral evil is the result of human choices, not divine cruelty. The theology of the cross: God does not stand apart from suffering but entered into it through Jesus Christ (Psalm 22:1 is quoted by Jesus on the cross, showing God understands abandonment). Soul-making response: suffering enables moral and spiritual development; a world of no challenge would prevent the growth of virtues such as courage and compassion. Islamic perspective: trials test and purify faith; Allah’s mercy (‘Ar-Rahim’) encompasses even suffering.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources or thinkers; clear weighing of arguments (e.g. noting which type of evil each response handles best); justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides presented with some development and at least one source; conclusion present.
Developing: Both sides attempted but unevenly developed; limited use of sources; conclusion may be weak.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; few or no sources; little to no conclusion. [15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Explain two different ways in which Christians understand God's relationship with the world.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per way): 1 mark for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with source. Example responses: (1) God as transcendent — utterly beyond and outside the universe, not directly involved in earthly events; some denominations, particularly in the Reformed tradition, emphasise God’s sovereignty and otherness. (2) God as immanent — personally present and active in the world; the Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32) depicts a God who runs to meet returning sinners; the Holy Spirit is understood as God’s continuing presence in believers’ lives. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State the name of the Jewish declaration of faith that affirms G-d is One.
practice_questions.marks: The Shema [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Jews mean when they say G-d is both transcendent and immanent.
practice_questions.marks: Transcendent: G-d exists beyond and outside the created world, above time and space [1 mark]. Immanent: G-d is also present within the world and involved in human lives, for example guiding the Israelites in the wilderness [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning and significance of the Shekinah in Judaism.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: The Shekinah refers to G-d’s manifest or dwelling presence (1 mark); the term first appears in the Talmud, not the Hebrew Bible itself (1 mark); it is associated with the pillar of cloud and fire in Exodus (e.g. Exodus 40:35) (1 mark); in Kabbalistic thought it is linked with the Sefirot and the feminine aspects of G-d (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Jewish beliefs about the nature of G-d are expressed in scripture and tradition.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• G-d as One: the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the central declaration of monotheism, recited daily; it affirms that G-d is absolutely singular and undivided, shaping all Jewish worship and identity.
• G-d as Creator: Genesis 1:1 states G-d created the heavens and the earth; this means the universe depends entirely on G-d and humans (Genesis 1:27 — made in G-d’s image) have a special relationship with the Creator.
• G-d as Judge: on Rosh Hashannah, Jews believe G-d evaluates each person’s deeds over the past year; this motivates Jews to repent and live righteously.
• The Shekinah: described in Exodus as the cloud filling the Tabernacle (Exodus 40:35), it represents G-d’s immanent presence; in Kabbalistic thought the Sefirot further explain how G-d interacts with the world.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per belief — 1 for naming, 2 for explaining, 3 for developing with a source of wisdom]

practice_questions.text: 'The Shekinah proves that G-d is more immanent than transcendent in Judaism.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Shekinah describes G-d’s actual dwelling presence among the Israelites (Exodus 13:20–22; 40:35), suggesting closeness rather than distance.
• Kabbalistic understanding of the Sefirot places the Shekinah as G-d’s presence within the created world, emphasising immanence.
• Genesis 1:27 (humans created in G-d’s image) reinforces the idea of an intimate relationship between G-d and humanity.
• G-d’s intervention in history (the Exodus, giving the Torah) shows active involvement in human affairs.

Arguments against:
• The Shema and Jewish tradition strongly emphasise G-d’s absolute transcendence — G-d is beyond the universe, not contained within it.
• The Book of Job illustrates that G-d’s ways are incomprehensible to humans, suggesting distance rather than closeness.
• The Shekinah’s appearance as cloud and fire is itself a sign of G-d’s transcendence — G-d cannot be seen directly; only a manifestation is visible.
• Orthodox Judaism stresses that G-d is entirely unlike anything in creation and resists too much emphasis on immanence as potentially reducing G-d to a human scale.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Deuteronomy 6:4; Exodus 40:35; Book of Job; Genesis 1:27), explicit weighing of which argument is stronger, justified conclusion noting the tension between immanence and transcendence as central to Jewish thought.
Secure: Clear arguments on both sides with some source reference; concludes with a reasoned judgement.
Developing: One side more developed than the other; some source reference; basic conclusion.
Emerging: Only one perspective given; little or no source reference; limited or no conclusion.
[15 marks — SPaG assessed on this response]

practice_questions.text: Outline Jewish responses to the problem of evil and suffering.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Free will — G-d gave humans freedom, which allows moral evil (1 mark); the Book of Job shows G-d’s ways are beyond human understanding (1 mark); the Book of Jonah illustrates G-d’s mercy even toward wrongdoers (1 mark); some Jewish thinkers argue suffering can refine a person spiritually (1 mark); progressive Jewish theologians have revisited beliefs after the Holocaust (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State one of the four margas in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks:
Any one of the following for 1 mark:
• Jnana yoga (the path of knowledge)
• Bhakti yoga (the path of devotion)
• Karma yoga (the path of selfless action)
• Raja yoga / Astanga yoga (the path of meditation)
[1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by karma yoga.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Karma yoga is the path of selfless or desireless action.
• The practitioner fulfils their duties without attachment to the results of those actions.
• It is based on the teaching in Bhagavad Gita II 47 that one has a right to action but not to its fruits.
• Actions performed this way do not generate karma that binds the person to samsara.
[1 mark for a basic description; 2 marks for a developed description that includes the idea of non-attachment or links to karma/samsara.]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning of varnashramadharma for Hindus.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Varnashramadharma combines varna (social grouping) and ashrama (stage of life) with dharma (duty).
• It defines the specific duties a Hindu should follow according to their social role and life stage.
• The four ashramas are: student, householder, forest dweller/retiree, and renunciant.
• Different margas are associated with different ashramas: e.g. karma yoga in the householder stage, raja yoga in the renunciant stage.
• Different traditions interpret varna either as hereditary birth categories or as descriptions of spiritual qualities.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for some development; 3 marks for a clear, developed outline that names specific ashramas or links to a second concept.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the four margas reflect Hindu beliefs about the path to moksha.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Jnana yoga reflects the belief that ignorance (avidya) about the true nature of reality is the root cause of rebirth in samsara. By studying scripture and meditating on the relationship between atman and Brahman, the jnana yogi dissolves this ignorance and achieves liberation. This path is supported by the Upanishads and by the Advaita Vedanta of Shankaracharya.
• Bhakti yoga reflects the belief that loving surrender to God can lead to moksha. Bhagavad Gita IX 26-28 teaches that Krishna accepts sincere devotion from all, regardless of caste or gender, suggesting that moksha is not restricted to the learned but is accessible to all through the heart.
• Karma yoga reflects the belief that action itself is not the problem — it is selfish desire attached to action that binds one to samsara. Bhagavad Gita II 47 teaches that desireless action (nishkam karma) does not accumulate karma and therefore moves the actor towards moksha.
• Raja yoga reflects the belief that the mind must be stilled through meditation to perceive the true self. Samadhi, the highest stage of Patanjali's eight-limbed path, is the experiential union with Brahman that constitutes moksha whilst still living.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per way — 1 for identifying the marga, 2 for explaining the connection to moksha, 3 for developing the explanation with a named source or concept.]

practice_questions.text: 'Bhakti yoga is the most important path to moksha in Hinduism.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Bhakti yoga is the most widely practised marga in popular Hinduism, suggesting it resonates most deeply with the majority of believers. Temples, festivals and devotional singing (bhajan and kirtan) all express bhakti.
• Bhagavad Gita IX 26-28 presents Krishna as personally welcoming bhakti: he teaches that offering even simple gifts with devotion is acceptable, implying bhakti is the most direct relationship with the divine.
• The Vaishnavite philosopher Ramanuja argued that bhakti is the highest path because it maintains a loving relationship between the self and Brahman rather than dissolving the self. For Ramanuja, this personal relationship is the ultimate spiritual reality.
• The medieval Bhakti Movement (Mirabai, Tukaram, Kabir) showed that bhakti crosses caste and gender barriers, making it the most inclusive and therefore most universally important path.

Arguments against:
• Jnana yoga tradition, especially Advaita Vedanta (Shankaracharya), holds that knowledge is the highest path because it directly removes avidya (ignorance), the root cause of samsara. Devotion is valuable but remains within the world of maya until knowledge transcends it.
• Karma yoga, as taught in Bhagavad Gita II 47 and lived by Gandhi, can be argued to be most important because it engages with the world rather than withdrawing from it. Social action (sewa, dana) expresses Hindu values in everyday life.
• Raja yoga’s goal of samadhi (direct experiential union with Brahman) could be seen as the most complete realisation of moksha, surpassing even devotion in depth.
• Hindu teaching broadly accepts that all four margas are equally valid and that the idea of one being “most important” misrepresents the tradition’s inclusive approach to liberation.

Mastering: Both sides developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita II 47; IX 26-28; Ramanuja; Shankaracharya); explicit comparison of margas; a reasoned, justified conclusion that engages with the word “most important.”
Secure: Two clear sides with some development; at least one named source; a conclusion that takes a position.
Developing: One side better developed than the other; limited source use; a partial conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; no or incorrect sources; no real conclusion.
[15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning of svadharma and explain how it relates to karma yoga.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Svadharma means personal or individual duty — the specific obligations appropriate to one’s own social role, life stage and spiritual capacity.
• Karma yoga teaches that performing one’s own duties without attachment to the results does not bind the actor to samsara.
• Bhagavad Gita II 47 states: ‘You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions.’
• Together, svadharma and karma yoga mean that every person has a unique set of duties, and fulfilling those duties selflessly is itself a spiritual path.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for linking svadharma to karma yoga; 3 marks for a developed answer that includes a source or example such as Gandhi.]

before.exam_tip_html: The 15-mark Discuss questions on this topic often ask whether one marga is more important than others, or whether selfless action or devotion is the best path to moksha. When you Discuss, present both sides: for example, jnana yoga proponents argue that wisdom directly removes the ignorance causing samsara, while bhakti traditions (especially Ramanuja) counter that love for God is the highest form of realisation. Name specific sources — Bhagavad Gita II 47 for karma yoga, IX 26–28 for bhakti yoga — to access the top mark band. A common student error is treating the four margas as mutually exclusive; examiners reward candidates who show that Hinduism allows — even encourages — following more than one simultaneously. Check the spelling of technical terms: varnashramadharma, svadharma, moksha and nishkam karma are all assessed in SPaG on the extended response.

practice_questions.text: State one condition that Thomas Aquinas identified as necessary for a just war.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: legitimate authority / just cause / right intention. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the term 'Holy War'.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that identify: a war believed to be commanded or sanctioned by God (1 mark); fought in defence of religious belief or sacred territory, claiming divine authorisation rather than relying on human moral criteria (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three religious teachings that could be used to argue against violence.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct points, for example: Jesus's command to 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:43-44) suggests violence towards others is wrong; Micah 4:3 envisions nations beating swords into ploughshares, suggesting peace is the religious ideal; mainstream Islamic scholars teach that killing innocent civilians is strictly forbidden under Islamic law and is a grave sin. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Just War Theory is challenged by modern forms of warfare.
practice_questions.marks: Credit two developed points, for example: Technological warfare using drones raises the question of proportionality — precision weapons may reduce civilian casualties but the ease of deploying them may lower the moral threshold for using force, which Just War's 'last resort' condition resists (3 marks). Apocalyptic or nuclear warfare cannot satisfy Just War's requirement to spare non-combatants, because nuclear weapons cause indiscriminate mass destruction — no military objective could be proportionate to this harm, leading many religious leaders to call for nuclear disarmament (3 marks). [6 marks — 3 marks per point: 1 basic, 2 developed, 3 developed with religious reference]

practice_questions.text: 'Religion always causes violence rather than preventing it.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Religious language has been used to legitimise terrorism and atrocity throughout history, from the Crusades to modern extremist groups who claim divine sanction; the concept of Holy War can encourage believers to think ordinary moral limits do not apply when God commands violence; passages such as Joel 3:9-11 and Joshua 8:1 have been used to justify aggressive war; religious identity differences can harden divisions between communities, raising the risk of conflict.

Arguments against: Most religious traditions explicitly teach that violence is a last resort or is forbidden: Jesus commands love of enemies (Matthew 5:43-44); Micah 4:3 envisions a world without weapons; Islamic scholars condemn terrorism as a distortion of faith; Just War Theory was developed precisely to restrain rather than encourage war; religious peacemakers such as Gandhi, Desmond Tutu and Martin Luther King Jr used their faith as the motivation for non-violent resistance; many religious organisations run reconciliation and aid programmes in conflict zones.

Mastering: Both sides are fully developed with named sources, explicit weighing of the arguments and a justified conclusion (e.g. religion is sometimes misused to justify violence but its dominant teachings and most prominent practitioners have worked for peace).
Secure: Both sides covered with some named teachings and a conclusion.
Developing: Some attempt at both sides; limited use of religious evidence.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no use of religious teaching. [15 marks + SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between conventional, technological and apocalyptic warfare.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct points: Conventional warfare involves armies in direct combat and was the context in which Just War Theory was originally developed; technological warfare uses drones or precision weapons at a distance, raising questions about proportionality and the ease of deploying force; apocalyptic warfare, such as nuclear weapons, involves indiscriminate mass destruction that cannot distinguish between combatants and civilians. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term ‘Nibbana’ in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of the following: the end of suffering / the extinguishing of craving, hatred and delusion / the ultimate goal of Buddhist practice / the state the Buddha reached at Enlightenment. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Four Sights that led Siddhattha Gotama to renounce his princely life.
practice_questions.marks: Students should describe the four encounters: an old man (showing the reality of old age), a sick man (showing the reality of illness), a corpse (showing the reality of death), and a wandering ascetic/holy man (suggesting that a spiritual path exists). 1 mark: naming two or more sights correctly. 2 marks: describing all four with a brief explanation of their significance. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Three Marks of Existence in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per Mark of Existence, each requiring a name plus a brief explanation:
• Dukkha—suffering or unsatisfactoriness; all conditioned existence is unsatisfying.
• Anicca—impermanence; all conditioned things change and cannot last.
• Anatta—no fixed self; there is no permanent, independent soul.
[3 marks, 1 per correctly outlined Mark]

practice_questions.text:
Explain how the teaching of dependent origination is connected to the Buddhist understanding of samsara.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Dependent origination (paticca-samuppada) teaches that everything arises from conditions—including rebirth. Because ignorance conditions mental formations, and so on through the 12 nidanas, beings are caught in the cycle of birth, ageing and death (samsara).
• The 12 links map how ignorance in a past life gives rise, through a chain of conditions, to a present life, which in turn conditions future existence.
• The Tibetan Wheel of Life illustrates how beings cycle through existence driven by the three poisons at the hub of the wheel.
• Because samsara is conditioned by ignorance and craving, it can cease when those conditions are removed, showing the path to liberation is logically possible.
• The Majjhima Nikaya 22 (Alagaddupama Sutta) records the Buddha as teaching that he only teaches suffering and its ending, which dependent origination makes possible.
Mastering: both the logic of conditionality and its link to samsara are explained clearly with named teaching references and explicit analysis of the relationship.
Secure: conditionality and samsara are connected with a named reference and some development.
Developing: a basic link made between dependent origination and rebirth with limited development.
Emerging: a simple point about dependent origination or samsara with no clear connection. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The most important thing the Buddha taught was that there is no permanent self.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Anatta (no fixed self) is unique to Buddhism and challenges the widespread human assumption that a permanent ‘I’ exists. If the belief in a permanent self is the root of craving, then understanding anatta is the key to ending all suffering.
• Theravada Buddhism teaches that the five khandas (aggregates) are what people mistake for a ‘self’, and seeing through this illusion is essential for Nibbana.
• The Dhammapada (35–36) links controlling the mind—which includes the illusion of self—to liberation. Without anatta, the Buddhist path makes less logical sense.
• Mahayana Buddhism extends this with sunyata, suggesting that emptiness of self is fundamental to all Buddhist metaphysics.

Arguments against or offering a different priority:
• The Four Noble Truths could be seen as the most important teaching: they provide the overall diagnosis (dukkha), cause (tanha), cure (Nibbana) and method (the Eightfold Path), of which anatta is just one supporting idea.
• The Dhamma itself—and specifically dependent origination (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)—might be considered the most important, as it explains why anatta is true; anatta follows from conditionality.
• For many lay Buddhists, the Five Precepts and ethical practice are the most practically important teachings in daily life.
• Theravada and Mahayana interpret anatta somewhat differently; some Mahayana schools speak of a ‘buddha-nature’ that complicates a straightforward ‘no-self’ reading, suggesting the teaching is more nuanced than the statement implies.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Dhammapada 35–36, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, reference to Theravada/Mahayana distinction), explicit weighing of arguments and a justified conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered with at least one named source and a clear conclusion.
Developing: some argument on both sides but limited use of sources and a weak conclusion.
Emerging: one-sided response with no sources and little or no conclusion. [15 marks, SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Describe the importance of the Dhamma as one of the Three Jewels of Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: Students should identify that the Three Jewels are the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, and explain the significance of the Dhamma: it represents both the eternal truth and the Buddha’s teachings; Buddhists take refuge in the Dhamma as their guide to liberation. 1 mark: identifying the Dhamma as one of the Three Jewels. 2 marks: explaining its significance as both truth and teaching that guides Buddhists toward Nibbana. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: State the Pali term for the Second Noble Truth about the cause of suffering.
practice_questions.marks: Samudaya (also accept tanha as the named cause, or 'the arising of suffering'). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Buddhists mean by tanha.
practice_questions.marks: Tanha means craving or thirst; it is compulsive, grasping desire—not ordinary preference—that arises from delusion about what can bring lasting satisfaction. 1 mark: identifying tanha as craving/desire. 2 marks: explaining that it is compulsive/grasping and identified as the cause of suffering. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the three types of suffering described in the First Noble Truth.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per type of suffering, each requiring the Pali term and a brief explanation:
• Dukkha-dukkha—obvious physical and mental pain such as illness, injury and grief.
• Viparinama-dukkha—the suffering that arises when pleasant things change or end.
• Sankhara-dukkha—the deep, all-pervasive unsatisfactoriness of all conditioned existence. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the role of the three poisons in causing suffering according to Buddhist teaching.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The three poisons are Lobha (attachment/greed), Dosa (aversion/hatred) and Moha (ignorance/delusion). They are the root causes of tanha and therefore of all suffering.
• Moha is the most fundamental poison because it is ignorance of the true nature of reality (impermanence, no-self) that gives rise to both Lobha and Dosa.
• When we wrongly believe things can give permanent satisfaction, Lobha arises; when we wrongly believe things can be permanent threats, Dosa arises.
• The Tibetan Wheel of Life depicts the three poisons as a pig, snake and bird at the hub, showing how they fuel the cycle of samsara.
• The Dhammapada (334–336) warns that craving, if not eliminated, will overgrow the person.
• Removing the three poisons through the Eightfold Path is what ends suffering.
Mastering: all three poisons explained with their role in generating tanha, named references used, clear causal chain shown.
Secure: two or three poisons explained with a named reference and development.
Developing: basic description of the three poisons with limited explanation of how they cause suffering.
Emerging: names one or two poisons without explanation. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The most important of the three poisons is Moha (ignorance).'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Moha is the foundational poison: both Lobha (greed) and Dosa (hatred) are said to arise from ignorance about the true nature of reality—specifically, the mistaken belief in a permanent self and in things that can provide lasting satisfaction.
• If Moha were removed, Lobha and Dosa would have no ground in which to grow. Eliminating ignorance is therefore the most direct path to ending all suffering.
• Buddhist practice—especially meditation and the cultivation of wisdom (panna)—specifically targets ignorance, suggesting the tradition itself views Moha as the primary problem.
• The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11) places ignorance at the start of the chain of dependent origination, confirming its priority.

Arguments against or offering a different emphasis:
• In practice, many Buddhists find Lobha (craving/attachment) the most destructive poison in daily life; attachment to people, pleasure and possessions causes obvious suffering and is the everyday form of tanha.
• Dosa (hatred and aversion) leads to harmful actions that damage individuals and communities; some might argue that reducing hatred has the most immediate beneficial impact.
• Theravada teaching describes Moha, Lobha and Dosa as interdependent—they constantly reinforce one another, so prioritising one over the others may be misleading.
• The Dhammapada (334–336) focuses specifically on craving (Lobha/tanha) as the creeper that overgrows the person, suggesting the tradition sometimes foregrounds attachment rather than ignorance.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammapada 334–336), explicit weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered with at least one named reference and a clear conclusion.
Developing: some argument on each side with limited sources and a weak conclusion.
Emerging: one-sided response with no sources. [15 marks, SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the three types of tanha identified in the Second Noble Truth.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per type of tanha, each requiring identification and a brief explanation:
• Kama-tanha—craving for sensory pleasure; the desire for pleasant sensory experiences.
• Bhava-tanha—craving for continued existence or becoming; the desire for rebirth or for things to continue.
• Vibhava-tanha—craving for non-existence or annihilation; the desire to escape existence entirely rather than following the Buddhist path. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what Havdalah marks in Jewish practice.
practice_questions.marks: The end of Shabbat / the separation of Shabbat from the rest of the week. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the Seder meal at Pesach.
practice_questions.marks: The Haggadah is read to retell the story of the Exodus from Egypt [1] and symbolic foods including matzah, bitter herbs and salt water are eaten to recall the experience of slavery and liberation [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of Yom Kippur for Jewish people.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: Yom Kippur is the holiest day in the Jewish calendar; it involves a 25-hour fast during which five physical pleasures are forbidden; worshippers recite the Vidui (confession) and seek Kapparah (atonement); the Neilah service closes the day with a blast of the shofar; Jews believe the Book of Life is sealed on this day. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Shabbat is observed differently by Orthodox and Reform Jews.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Orthodox Jews follow all 39 prohibited categories of work strictly (e.g. no electricity, no driving), believing these derive from the binding Oral Law and reflect the command in Exodus 20:8-11 to 'keep it holy'. Reform Jews may drive to synagogue, seeing communal worship as more important than technical restrictions.
• In Orthodox communities, the mechitzah (partition) separates men and women at synagogue Shabbat services. Reform synagogues allow mixed seating and women to lead services.
• Both communities share Kiddush, candle lighting and the Shabbat meal, but Orthodox Jews require a minyan of ten men for services; Reform congregations may count women.
[6 marks — 3 marks per difference: 1 for a simple statement, 2 for development, 3 for a relevant source]

practice_questions.text: 'Yom Kippur is the most important Jewish festival.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Yom Kippur is universally regarded as the holiest day (Yom HaKippurim — the Day of Atonements); the full 25-hour fast and five prohibitions show its supreme solemnity.
• The concept of Kapparah and the sealing of the Book of Life make it unique: no other festival carries this weight of judgement and forgiveness.
• Synagogue attendance on Yom Kippur is highest of any day, including among Jews who rarely attend otherwise, showing its central place in Jewish identity.
• Teshuva enables Jews to repair relationships with G-d and with each other in a way no other festival provides.

Arguments against:
• Shabbat is described in Genesis 2:1-3 and the Ten Commandments as the holiest recurring time; Yom Kippur is annual, Shabbat weekly — many rabbis argue Shabbat outweighs all other festivals in obligation.
• Pesach celebrates the defining event of Jewish history — the Exodus from Egypt — and the Seder meal has been practised continuously for millennia. Exodus 12:14-15 calls it 'a lasting ordinance'.
• Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are closely linked; it is arguably the pair that matters, not Yom Kippur alone.
• Sukkot and Shavuot have equal biblical status as Pilgrim Festivals, all commanded in Torah.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Genesis 2:1-3, Exodus 20:8-11, Exodus 12:14-15, Leviticus 23), different festival traditions compared, and a justified conclusion explaining which festival is most fundamental to Jewish identity.
Secure: Clear arguments on both sides with relevant named sources and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points with limited source reference; conclusion present but not fully argued.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; little or no source material used. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline three rituals associated with Rosh Hashanah.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: blowing the shofar up to 100 times during the synagogue service; Tashlich — casting breadcrumbs into flowing water to symbolise casting away sins; eating apples dipped in honey to symbolise hope for a sweet new year; eating pomegranates representing the wish to fulfil many commandments; Teshuva — reflecting on wrongdoing and resolving to repent over the ten days to Yom Kippur. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

practice_questions.text: State one festival celebrated by Theravada Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: Wesak / Vassa / Uposatha Days / Kathina. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the lay sangha in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: The lay sangha are Buddhists who live as householders rather than monastics [1]; they observe the Five Precepts, support monks and nuns through offerings (dana), perform puja and attend festivals [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of Wesak for Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Wesak commemorates the three most important events in the Buddha's life — his birth, enlightenment and Parinibbana [1]; it is the most widely celebrated Buddhist festival, observed across Theravada and Mahayana traditions [1]; Buddhists mark it with offerings, meditation, chanting and acts of generosity, renewing their commitment to the Buddhist path [1]. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Sangha is important to Buddhists.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Sangha is one of the Three Jewels — without the community of practitioners, the Dhamma cannot be preserved and transmitted. Taking refuge in the Sangha (the Three Refuges) is a foundational act of Buddhist commitment.
• The monastic sangha provides teaching, preserves the Vinaya and Dhamma, and offers a model of dedicated practice. The Dhammapada 360–369 praises the qualities of a well-restrained monastic, showing the spiritual authority the Sangha holds.
• The Sangha provides lay Buddhists with a community for festival observance, Uposatha days and support — reducing isolation and fostering collective commitment to the path.
[6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 simple point, 2 developed, 3 with teaching/source]

practice_questions.text: 'The monastic sangha is more important to Buddhism than the lay sangha.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The monastic sangha preserves the Vinaya and Dhamma, trains future teachers and provides the model of full-time dedicated practice; without it, Buddhist teachings would be lost.
• Monks and nuns observe the Ten Precepts, living a life of greater renunciation than lay Buddhists, which is traditionally seen as generating greater spiritual progress and merit.
• The Buddha himself was a monastic who modelled renunciation; the Sangha he established began with monks (the first five disciples at Sarnath), not householders.

Arguments against:
• The lay sangha sustains the monastic community materially through alms, offerings and donations; without lay support, monasteries cannot function.
• The Dhammapada 360–369 praises restraint without limiting this to monastics; in Mahayana traditions, dedicated lay practitioners (such as the famous layman Vimalakirti) are considered equally capable of achieving high spiritual attainment.
• In contemporary Western Buddhism, lay-led communities are numerically dominant; defining the lay sangha as secondary marginalises the majority of Buddhists.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources and Theravada/Mahayana contrast; weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides presented with some Buddhist teaching; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited teaching reference.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little Buddhist content. [15 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the importance of Vassa (the Rain Retreat) for Theravada Buddhists.
