practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Vassa is a three-month rains retreat during which Theravada monks must remain in their monastery [1]; it is a period of intensive meditation and Dhamma study, allowing monastics to deepen their practice away from travel [1]; lay Buddhists increase their support through additional offerings and may observe extra precepts, strengthening the bond between monastic and lay communities [1]. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what Christians mean by 'original sin'.
practice_questions.marks: The idea that all humans inherit a tendency towards sin from Adam / humans are born with a bias towards sin / sin passed down from the Fall. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between natural evil and moral evil.
practice_questions.marks: Natural evil: evil caused by natural events such as earthquakes, disease or floods, not by human choice. [1 mark] Moral evil: evil caused by the free choices of human beings, such as war, murder or cruelty. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the role of the Word in John 1.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks from: the Word (Logos) was with God and was God from the beginning [1]; all things were made through the Word [1]; John identifies the Word as Jesus [1]; this establishes Jesus's pre-existence as divine before his birth [1].

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Christian responses to the problem of evil and suffering.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- The Free Will defence: God gave humans genuine freedom; to prevent evil would remove the freedom that makes love possible. The Fall (Genesis 3:1-19) shows how Free Will was first misused, but God did not override it. [up to 3 marks]
- The example of Job: the book of Job shows that suffering can be beyond human understanding; God's response from the whirlwind stresses that his purposes are greater than what humans can see. [up to 3 marks]
- Suffering leads to spiritual growth; some Christians argue natural evil and suffering build character and deepen faith.
- The Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9-15) includes a petition for forgiveness and deliverance from evil, suggesting God hears and responds to suffering. [3 marks per point: 1 simple, 2 developed, 3 developed with source]

practice_questions.text: 'The existence of natural evil makes it impossible to believe in an all-powerful, loving God.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Natural evil (earthquakes, cancer, floods) is not caused by human Free Will, so the Free Will defence does not explain it.
- If God is omnipotent he could prevent natural disasters; if he is benevolent he would want to. The fact that he does not creates a logical problem.
- The suffering of innocent children (e.g. from disease) seems incompatible with a perfectly loving God.

Arguments against / alternative views:
- The Free Will defence addresses moral evil, but many Christians argue natural evil may serve purposes humans cannot fully see (Romans 8).
- The book of Job shows that suffering can occur without being punishment; God's ways are beyond human comprehension.
- Some Christians take a metaphorical view of Genesis and see the natural world as still 'very good' in its overall design, even if individual events cause suffering.
- Natural evil may be a consequence of the Fall on creation as a whole (the ‘cosmic fall’ interpretation), not a separate problem.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Genesis 3, book of Job, Romans 8); explicit weighing with a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with at least one source; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources; conclusion present but not fully weighed.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; no real use of sources; no justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two different Christian interpretations of the Genesis creation account.
practice_questions.marks: Literal interpretation: Genesis is historically and scientifically accurate; the world was created in six 24-hour days. [1 mark] Metaphorical interpretation: Genesis is theological poetry conveying who created the world and why, not how or when; science and faith are compatible. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one promise G-d made to Abraham in the Covenant found in Genesis 12:1–3.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: a special relationship with G-d / many descendants (a great nation) / the Promised Land of Canaan [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of Moses in the Covenant at Sinai.
practice_questions.marks: Moses received the Torah and the Ten Commandments from G-d at Mount Sinai [1 mark]; he acted as the intermediary between G-d and the Israelite people, conveying G-d's laws and obligations to them [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Jews believe about the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: The Messiah (Hebrew: mashiach) is an anointed leader descended from King David (1 mark); the Messiah will bring world peace and an end to warfare (e.g. Micah 4:1–3) (1 mark); the Messiah will gather the Jewish people from exile and rebuild the Temple (1 mark); Elijah is expected to return to announce the Messiah's arrival (1 mark); Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah whereas Progressive Jews may interpret this collectively (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Covenant with Abraham is significant for Jewish belief and practice today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The promise of the Promised Land (Genesis 12:1–3) continues to shape Jewish attitudes to the State of Israel — many Zionist Jews see the establishment of Israel in 1948 as the fulfilment of the covenant promise, supported by Isaiah 11:11–12 which speaks of G-d gathering scattered Israel.
• The sign of the covenant — circumcision — is still practised today in the ceremony of Brit Milah, marking Jewish male identity and continuity with Abraham.
• The covenant established the idea of the Jewish people as specially chosen by G-d, which shapes Jewish self-understanding as a people with a particular religious purpose and responsibility.
• The promise of descendants gives Jews confidence in G-d’s faithfulness across generations, sustaining Jewish identity through historical persecution.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per significance — 1 for naming, 2 for explaining, 3 for developing with a source]

practice_questions.text: 'The Covenant at Sinai is more important than the Covenant with Abraham for Jewish life today.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Ten Commandments from the Covenant at Sinai (Exodus 20:2–17) form the foundation of Jewish law and ethics, directly shaping how Jews live every day.
• The Sinai Covenant gave the whole Torah — 613 mitzvot — which regulates Jewish daily life far more comprehensively than the Abrahamic covenant.
• Moses is the greatest prophet in Judaism; the Sinai Covenant represents the defining moment of G-d’s revelation to the Jewish people as a whole.
• The weekly Shabbat, Jewish festivals and dietary laws all flow directly from the Sinai Covenant.

Arguments against:
• The Abrahamic Covenant established Jewish identity and the concept of chosenness before any law was given; without it, the Sinai Covenant would have no people to be given to.
• The promise of the Promised Land (Genesis 12:1–3) remains highly relevant today in relation to the State of Israel and Jewish homeland identity.
• Circumcision, the sign of the Abrahamic Covenant, continues to be practised by the vast majority of Jewish families across all denominations.
• The Abrahamic Covenant’s promise of descendants sustains Jewish hope for the future, including the coming of the Messiah from the line of David.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Exodus 20; Genesis 12; Micah 4:1–3; Isaiah 11:11–12), explicit weighing, justified conclusion that recognises both covenants as essential but may distinguish their different emphases.
Secure: Clear two-sided argument with some sources; reasoned conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources; simple conclusion.
Emerging: One perspective only; no sources; no clear conclusion.
[15 marks — SPaG assessed on this response]

practice_questions.text: Outline different Jewish views on the nature of the Messiah and the Messianic Age.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah — a human leader from the line of David — who will restore the Temple and gather all Jews (1 mark); the Messianic Age will be an era of universal peace (Micah 4:1–3) (1 mark); Progressive Jews interpret the Messianic Age as a collective human achievement guided by Jewish values rather than the work of a single individual (1 mark); some ultra-Orthodox Jews reject the State of Israel because only the Messiah should establish a Jewish state (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what the Catholic Church means by an annulment.
practice_questions.marks: An official declaration that a supposed marriage was never valid (and therefore never truly existed). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Islam teaches about divorce.
practice_questions.marks: Credit any two developed points: divorce is permitted but described as 'the most disliked of all permitted things'; the husband may pronounce talaq; a waiting period (iddah) is required; women can seek khul' (divorce initiated by the wife). [1 mark per point, 2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Outline Christian teachings about the roles of men and women in marriage.
practice_questions.marks: Credit three developed points from within Christianity. Examples: Colossians 3:18-19 urges wives to submit to husbands and husbands to love their wives; Ephesians 5:25 calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church (servant leadership); 1 Timothy 2:11-14 has been used to restrict women's authority; egalitarians point to Galatians 3:28 as establishing full equality in Christ. [1 mark per point, 3 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two different religious attitudes to the religious upbringing of children.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Credit two well-developed points with supporting sources. Examples: Christianity holds that baptised parents make promises to raise children in the faith; the family is the 'domestic church' (Catholic Catechism). Islam requires parents to whisper the adhan at birth and teach children to pray; a child's religious formation is a parental duty. Non-religious perspectives argue that a religious upbringing can restrict children's freedom to form their own views. [3 marks per point: 1 simple point, 2 developed, 3 developed with source]

practice_questions.text: 'Divorce should never be acceptable to Christians.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (divorce should never be acceptable):
- Jesus said in Mark 10:11-12 that divorce followed by remarriage constitutes adultery, suggesting marriage is absolutely indissoluble.
- The Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be ended by divorce; this reflects God's permanent covenant love.
- 1 Corinthians 7:10-11 instructs a wife not to leave her husband; separation without remarriage may be the only option for an irretrievably broken marriage.
- Upholding the permanence of marriage protects children and the social fabric.

Arguments against (divorce can be acceptable):
- Matthew 5:32 includes an exception for sexual immorality, suggesting Jesus acknowledged some circumstances justify separation.
- Protestant traditions hold that God's grace extends to human failure; remarriage after divorce is accepted as a fresh start.
- Islam permits divorce, recognising that remaining in a harmful marriage can cause greater damage than ending it.
- Non-religious ethics prioritises the wellbeing of individuals; an unhappy or dangerous marriage is not worth preserving at all costs.

Mastering: Both sides argued with developed reasoning; named sources used; awareness of Catholic vs Protestant differences; Islam or non-religious perspective included; weighing of arguments; a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with some development; at least one source; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some arguments on both sides; limited sources; limited conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or minimal; no sources; no real conclusion. [15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which religious communities hold different views about the ordination of women.
practice_questions.marks: Credit two well-developed points. Examples: The Catholic and Orthodox churches restrict ordained priesthood to men, citing the example of Jesus's male apostles and 1 Timothy 2:11-14. Many Protestant denominations (Methodist, Anglican, Baptist) ordain women at all levels, citing Galatians 3:28 and arguing that restrictive texts were culturally conditioned responses to specific situations. [3 marks per point: 1 simple, 2 developed, 3 developed with source]

practice_questions.text: State one reason why a Christian might go on pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: to seek healing / to grow closer to God / to walk in the footsteps of biblical figures / to fulfil a vow / for spiritual renewal / to feel connected to the universal Church. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during a Christian Easter Sunday service.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Points may include: the service celebrates the resurrection of Jesus (1); a Paschal candle may be lit to symbolise Christ as the light of the world (1); the congregation may hear readings from Matthew 28 or Luke 24 (1); in Orthodox churches the declaration 'Christ is risen!' is shared (1); the Eucharist/Holy Communion is celebrated (1). Maximum 2 marks. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which a local church might support its community.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per valid way up to 3. Points may include: Sunday schools for children to learn the faith (1); youth clubs providing safe spaces for teenagers (1); mother-and-child groups supporting young families (1); visiting the elderly and sick (1); organising food banks or community events (1). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Christmas is important for Christians.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks per way. Points may include:
• Christmas celebrates the incarnation — God becoming human in Jesus. Luke 2:1-20 describes the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, which Christians believe shows God's love for humanity and his willingness to enter human experience (3).
• The visit of the Magi in Matthew 2:1-12 reinforces Jesus's universal significance — wise men from other nations recognise him as King of the Jews, showing salvation is for all people (3).
• Christmas strengthens community by bringing Christians together for services and family celebrations — sharing the joy of the incarnation and renewing commitment to faith (2).
• It is an opportunity for evangelism — carol services and nativity plays are often attended by non-churchgoers, giving Christians a chance to share the Gospel (2). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Pilgrimage is essential for Christian spiritual growth.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation with named sites (Lourdes, Jerusalem, Walsingham, Rome), specific benefits (healing, connection to salvation history) and clear denominational disagreement (Catholic/Orthodox value vs Protestant caution). Explains why some argue pilgrimage is essential (grace available at sacred sites, encounter with Christ's world) and why others disagree (God is everywhere; physical location is irrelevant; Bible does not command it). Justified conclusion that goes beyond 'it depends.' [13-15 marks]
Secure: Two developed arguments on each side with some reference to denominations or scripture; conclusion present. [9-12 marks]
Developing: Some relevant points, one side better developed; limited denominational comparison. [5-8 marks]
Emerging: Brief points with little development; no denominational comparison. [1-4 marks]
SPaG assessed on this question.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christian marriage and funeral rites reflect Christian beliefs about life and death.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks per way. Points may include:
• Marriage reflects the belief that human relationships mirror the relationship between Christ and the Church — Ephesians 5:31-33 describes marriage as a profound mystery, encouraging self-giving love modelled on Christ's love for believers (3).
• Christian funerals reflect the hope of resurrection — Jesus's words in John 11:25 ('I am the resurrection and the life') are commonly read at funerals, affirming that death is not the end and that believers will share in Christ's resurrection (3).
• The emphasis on forgiveness and thanksgiving in funeral services shows the Christian belief in grace — that life's meaning comes from relationship with God rather than achievements alone (2). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'absolute pacifism'.
practice_questions.marks: The belief that violence is always wrong in all circumstances and without exception. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which religious individuals or communities have worked for peace.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for two distinct points, for example: Martin Luther King Jr organised peaceful protests and marches to oppose racial segregation in the USA, drawing on his Christian faith; Quaker communities have actively campaigned with CND for nuclear disarmament, arguing nuclear weapons are morally unjustifiable. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three religious teachings or sources that support pacifism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct points, for example: The Quaker Declaration of 1660 states that Quakers 'utterly deny all outward wars and strife, and fightings with outward weapons'; Jesus teaches 'love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you' (Matthew 5:43-44); Matthew 5:38-42 challenges the principle of revenge, teaching people to 'turn the other cheek'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some religious believers adopt an absolute pacifist position.
practice_questions.marks: Credit two developed points, for example: Jesus's teaching in the Sermon on the Mount commands love of enemies and non-retaliation (Matthew 5:38-44) — absolute pacifists argue that if you genuinely love someone you cannot kill them, and that Christian ethics must embody God's kingdom values here and now regardless of practical consequences (3 marks). The Quaker tradition, grounded in the belief that there is 'that of God in every person', holds that killing any human being destroys a divine spark — therefore no cause or authority can justify war; the 1660 Declaration is their founding statement of this absolute commitment (3 marks). [6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 basic, 2 developed, 3 developed with teaching]

practice_questions.text: 'Non-violent action is always the best way to achieve peace and justice.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Gandhi's satyagraha campaigns achieved Indian independence without armed revolution; Martin Luther King's non-violent civil rights movement led to landmark legislation in the USA; the Sermon on the Mount teaches 'turn the other cheek' and 'love your enemies', suggesting that violence only perpetuates cycles of hatred; the Quaker Declaration 1660 argues all violence is a denial of God's presence in every person; non-violent action preserves the moral integrity of those using it.

Arguments against: Non-violent action is not always effective — it depends on an opponent who can be shamed or persuaded; against truly brutal regimes that simply massacre protesters, non-violence may allow injustice to continue; conditional pacifists argue force is sometimes the only way to protect the innocent; Just War Theory allows that some defensive wars are morally necessary; many religious believers do not accept absolute pacifism.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named individuals, scripture and theological argument; explicit weighing and justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides addressed with some named teachings and a conclusion.
Developing: Some attempt at both sides; limited evidence.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no religious teaching cited. [15 marks + SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between absolute pacifism and conditional pacifism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct differences: Absolute pacifism holds that violence is always wrong in every circumstance; conditional pacifism allows that violence may be a tragic last resort in extreme situations such as defending the innocent; absolute pacifists (such as Quakers) refuse to serve in any military capacity, whereas conditional pacifists may support just defensive wars. [3 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: For the 15-mark “Discuss” on pacifism, you need to present both absolute and conditional pacifist positions, not just argue one side. Name specific individuals (Gandhi, Martin Luther King, Desmond Tutu, Quaker Declaration 1660) and specific teachings (Matthew 5:38–42, Matthew 5:43–44). The most common error is treating all pacifists as holding the same view — examiners want to see you distinguish absolute from conditional pacifism. Spell “pacifism” and “non-violence” correctly; SPaG is assessed on your extended response.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'Loka' in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: A world, realm or plane of existence in Hindu cosmology. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Hindu understanding of the trigunas.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: the three fundamental qualities of prakriti/matter; tamas (inertia/darkness), rajas (energy/passion) and sattva (purity/clarity); everything in the universe is a mixture of these three; spiritual progress involves moving from tamas and rajas towards sattva. [2 marks — 1 for naming the gunas or giving a simple description, 2 for a more developed account]

practice_questions.text: Outline the roles of the Trimurti in the cycle of creation and destruction.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: the Trimurti consists of Brahma (creator), Vishnu (preserver) and Shiva (destroyer/regenerator); the universe moves through vast cycles called Mahayugas; at the end of each Mahayuga the universe is dissolved (pralaya) and then re-created; Brahma creates, Vishnu sustains and Shiva destroys in preparation for a new cycle; each figure has a corresponding realm (Brahma-Loka, Shiva-Loka, Vishnu-Loka/Vaikuntha). [3 marks — 1 for naming the Trimurti, 2 for explaining two roles, 3 for a full account including the Mahayuga cycle]

practice_questions.text: Explain the Hindu concepts of prakriti and purusha and their relationship to spiritual liberation.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Prakriti is primordial matter from which all physical and psychological realities emerge; purusha is pure consciousness or spirit; both are described in Bhagavad Gita XIII 19-20.
• When purusha mistakenly identifies with prakriti, it becomes bound in samsara; liberation comes from clearly discriminating between the two.
• The trigunas are the three qualities of prakriti (tamas, rajas, sattva) woven through all material existence; spiritual progress moves towards sattva and then beyond all three gunas.
[6 marks — 3 marks per concept: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a developed explanation with a source of wisdom]

practice_questions.text: 'The cyclical view of the universe in Hinduism makes human life meaningless.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments that could support the statement: if the universe endlessly cycles through creation and dissolution, individual lives may seem insignificant on a cosmic scale; the Kali Yuga (current age) is described as spiritually degenerate, which could produce pessimism; the vastness of the Mahayuga (4,320,000 years) dwarfs human existence.

Arguments that could challenge the statement: the human realm is described as rare and precious because moksha can be achieved from it; karma gives every action genuine moral weight and consequence; the cyclical universe is not fatalistic — individual choices in the present (kriyamana karma) always matter; bhakti traditions emphasise loving relationship with God (Vishnu/Vaikuntha) as giving life deep personal meaning; the Nasadiya Sukta's humility before mystery can inspire awe rather than nihilism; dharma (duty) structures meaningful engagement with life at every stage.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita XIII 19-20; Nasadiya Sukta), explicit weighing of arguments and a justified conclusion.
Secure: two clear perspectives with some use of Hindu teaching; conclusion present.
Developing: one side more developed; some relevant content; limited source use.
Emerging: one-sided or very brief; little specific Hindu content.

practice_questions.text: Outline what Hindus believe about the Devas and Asuras.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Devas are divine, luminous beings who enjoy great powers and inhabit higher realms; Asuras are powerful beings associated with ego, desire and spiritual darkness; both are part of the many-realm (Loka) cosmology of Hinduism; people can be born into realms inhabited by Devas or Asuras as a result of karma; even Deva existence is temporary unless moksha is achieved. [3 marks — 1 for identifying Devas/Asuras, 2 for contrasting them, 3 for linking their existence to karma and the wider cosmological picture]

practice_questions.text: State what the teleological argument attempts to prove.
practice_questions.marks: The teleological argument attempts to prove that God exists as the designer of the universe, based on the order and complexity found in the natural world. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the 'Anthropic principle' in the context of arguments for God's existence.
practice_questions.marks: The Anthropic principle observes that the physical conditions of the universe are precisely fine-tuned to permit life (1 mark); theists argue this fine-tuning is evidence of a creator who intended for conscious life to exist (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline two classical arguments that believers use to support the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark per argument identified (cosmological / first cause; teleological / design; moral argument; Anthropic principle; soul-making) up to 2, plus 1 mark for developing one (e.g. William Paley's watchmaker analogy shows that the complexity of the natural world implies a designer, just as a watch implies a watchmaker). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why some people find the design argument convincing.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per reason): 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a source. Example responses: (1) The order and complexity of the natural world suggests a designer — Paley argued in Natural Theology (1802) that just as a watch's complexity implies a watchmaker, the far greater complexity of living things implies God. (2) The Anthropic principle: the fine-tuning of physical constants to permit life is extremely unlikely by chance; Psalm 14:1 implies that recognising God in creation is reasonable ('The fool says in his heart, There is no God'). (3) The experience of awe and wonder at creation provides an intuitive sense of a creator that many find compelling alongside the rational argument. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Arguments for the existence of God are more convincing than arguments against.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: The First Cause / cosmological argument is supported by modern cosmology (the Big Bang shows the universe had a beginning; al-Ghazali's kalam: everything that begins has a cause). Paley's design argument: the complexity and order of living things is extraordinary; the Anthropic principle strengthens this with evidence of fine-tuning. The moral argument: the existence of objective moral values is best explained by a divine lawgiver. Many believers find the cumulative weight of these arguments, and the experience of awe and wonder, compelling evidence.

Arguments against: Hume: we cannot apply the analogy of a designed artefact to the whole universe; the cosmological argument commits the fallacy of composition. Darwin: natural selection explains complexity without a designer; Dawkins' 'Blind Watchmaker' removes the need for a divine designer of life. The moral argument fails if moral values can be explained through evolution or social contract. These arguments, at best, prove an uncaused first cause or designer — not the personal God of any specific religion.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named thinkers or sources; explicit weighing of the arguments (e.g. noting that the Anthropic principle addresses Darwin but not Hume); justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with some development and at least one source; conclusion present.
Developing: Both sides attempted but unevenly; limited sources; weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; few sources; little to no conclusion. [15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the ideas of 'soul-making' and 'awe and wonder' both support belief in a purposeful God.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per idea): 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a source. Soul-making (Irenaeus / John Hick): God designed the world not merely for pleasure but as an environment for moral and spiritual growth — challenges and even suffering serve the purpose of developing virtuous character; this implies the world has purpose rather than being an accident. Awe and wonder: the experience of encountering natural beauty, vastness or complexity prompts a sense that the universe points beyond itself to a creator; Genesis 1:31 notes God saw all he made was 'very good', supporting the view of a purposefully designed, good creation. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what Muslims must wear when entering the state of ihram during Hajj.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for: two white unstitched cloths (for men) / plain white garments / seamless white cloth. Accept: simple white clothing symbolising equality before Allah. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims do on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr).
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for any two of the following: they spend the night in extended prayer / recitation of the Qur'an / supplication (du'a) / some observe i'tikaf (retreat to the mosque for the last ten days of Ramadan) / they seek blessings on the night the Qur'an was first revealed. [2 marks — 1 per valid point]

practice_questions.text: Outline why the pilgrimage of Hajj is important for Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for a developed outline including: it is an obligatory Pillar for those who are able / it commemorates the trials of Ibrahim and his family / it symbolises equality before Allah (ihram) / it unites the global Muslim community (ummah) / it gives the individual an opportunity to seek forgiveness and spiritual renewal / it re-enacts key events connected to the origins of Islam. Award three marks for at least two of these points developed clearly. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Zakah is important for Muslims.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Zakah purifies a Muslim's wealth by acknowledging that all wealth belongs to Allah. Giving 2.5% of savings above the Nisab reminds Muslims that money is a trust from Allah and not something to be hoarded selfishly.
• Zakah reduces inequality and supports those in need — the Qur'an specifies eight categories of recipients including the poor, the indebted and travellers (Surah 9:60). This promotes social justice, a key Islamic value.
• Zakah strengthens community bonds by redistributing wealth to those who need it, reflecting the Muslim concept of ummah (global community).
• It is a divine command and one of the Five Pillars, so fulfilling it is an act of obedience to Allah.
Mastering: Two developed points each with a named source, clear explanation of significance.
Secure: Two developed points, at least one source.
Developing: Two basic points, limited sources or development.
Emerging: One point, brief. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Sawm (fasting) is the most spiritually demanding of the Five Pillars.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Sawm requires physical self-denial for an entire month — no food, drink or other physical pleasures from dawn to sunset — which demands extraordinary willpower and discipline.
• Fasting is an internal, invisible act that only Allah can see, making it a particularly sincere demonstration of submission. The Qur'an says it is decreed so that Muslims 'may become righteous' (Surah 2:183).
• The Night of Power within Ramadan is described as better than a thousand months, giving Sawm an unparalleled spiritual intensity.
• Fasting cultivates empathy with the poor and gratitude for Allah's blessings.

Arguments against:
• Hajj could be argued to be more demanding because it requires financial sacrifice, long travel, physical endurance and the performance of many rituals over several days. For many Muslims, it is a once-in-a-lifetime transformation.
• Salah is performed five times every single day of a Muslim's life, which could be seen as a more constant and pervasive spiritual discipline than a month of fasting.
• Zakah involves giving up real wealth permanently, which may be the hardest demand for those with limited means.
• The most spiritually demanding act is subjective and may depend on the individual Muslim's circumstances and strengths.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named Qur'anic references, explicit comparison of the Pillars, explicit weighing of arguments and a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed, at least one source, clear conclusion.
Developing: Both sides but limited development or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided, brief, minimal sources. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between Zakah and Khums.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for: Zakah is obligatory for both Sunni and Shi'a Muslims / set at 2.5% of savings above the Nisab / paid annually on eligible wealth. Khums is a Shi'a-only obligation / set at 20% (one fifth) of certain surplus earnings / paid to the Imam or his representatives. Award three marks for a developed contrast that clearly identifies both obligations and notes the Sunni/Shi'a distinction. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what Muslims mean by 'shirk'.
practice_questions.marks: Shirk means associating partners with Allah / attributing partners, equals or associates to Allah. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Muslim belief in Tawhid.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: Tawhid is the belief in the absolute oneness of Allah (1 mark); this means Allah is unique, undivided, without partner or equal, and that He alone is worthy of worship (1 mark for development, e.g. linking to Surah 112 or explaining what this rules out). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim as names of Allah.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks: both names derive from the Arabic root for mercy (1 mark); Ar-Rahman refers to Allah's universal mercy extended to all of creation (1 mark); Ar-Rahim refers to Allah's particular mercy directed especially towards believers (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muslims regard shirk as the most serious sin in Islam.
practice_questions.marks: Possible points: Shirk directly contradicts Tawhid, which is the foundation of all Islamic belief — to associate a partner with Allah is to reject the most fundamental truth about God's nature (1+1 mark). The Qur'an teaches that shirk is an unforgivable sin for someone who dies unrepentant, making it uniquely serious among all human failings (1+1 mark). Shirk directs worship away from Allah to something less, which is both a profound injustice and a form of ingratitude for the blessings of creation (1+1 mark). Surah 112 (al-Ikhlas) affirms that Allah 'neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent' — any claim to the contrary is therefore a denial of this revealed truth (1+1 mark for citing a source). [6 marks: 3 marks per reason — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'Tawhid makes it impossible for Muslims to respect other religious traditions.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Tawhid rules out polytheism as a form of shirk; the Christian Trinity is viewed as compromising Allah's oneness; Surah 112 directly addresses the claim that Allah 'begets' or has an equivalent; Islamic theology teaches that all previous religions were originally monotheistic but became corrupted — implying other traditions have deviated from truth. Arguments against: Islam teaches that Christians and Jews are 'People of the Book' who share prophets and scriptures with Muslims; the Qur'an calls for respectful dialogue; shirk is a theological category, not a personal moral judgement — Muslims can respect individuals while disagreeing with their beliefs; Islam teaches that all humans are born with the fitrah (natural inclination to monotheism), so other believers are not dismissed. Mastering: Both sides developed with named sources (Surah 112, Surah 53:19-25, 'People of the Book'), explicit weighing of theological disagreement vs practical respect, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with some sourcing; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or limited sourcing. Emerging: Brief, unsupported. [15 marks: SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: State which Surah of the Qur'an is most directly associated with expressing the oneness of Allah.
practice_questions.marks: Surah 112 / Surah al-Ikhlas. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'puja' in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks:
Any accurate one-sentence description for 1 mark. For example:
• Puja is a form of devotional worship offered to a deity image (murti), involving offerings such as flowers, incense, food and light.
[1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Hindus do during a havan ceremony.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A havan is a fire ceremony in which offerings such as ghee, grains and wood are made into a sacred fire.
• Sanskrit mantras are recited by a priest or family member as offerings are made.
• The fire is understood to carry offerings to the deities and to purify the participants.
• Havan is performed at life-cycle events such as weddings and at regular temple rituals.
[1 mark for a basic description; 2 marks for a developed description that includes the purpose or context of havan.]

practice_questions.text: Outline the importance of darshan for Hindu worshippers.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Darshan means ‘sight’ or ‘vision.’ When a worshipper stands before a murti, they understand themselves to be in the presence of the deity and to be seen by the deity.
• This mutual gaze is experienced as a blessing: the devotee comes to see God and to receive God’s gaze.
• Darshan also applies to holy people (gurus, sadhus): being in the presence of a spiritually advanced person is held to transmit blessings.
• Pilgrims travel great distances for the darshan of famous gurus or at celebrated temples.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for some development; 3 marks for a clear, developed outline that includes more than one form of darshan or explains the spiritual significance.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Varanasi is an important pilgrimage destination for Hindus.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Varanasi is situated on the banks of the sacred river Ganges, which is worshipped as the goddess Ganga. Bathing in the Ganges is believed to cleanse accumulated negative karma and to bring the soul closer to moksha. This makes the city the most spiritually powerful bathing place in Hinduism.
• Varanasi is considered the city of Shiva. Dying in Varanasi is believed to guarantee liberation (kashi labh) because Shiva is said to whisper the liberating mantra into the ear of the dying. Hindus therefore bring seriously ill relatives there to die, and the burning ghats are permanently alight with cremation fires.
• The Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas — the most sacred shrines to Shiva. Receiving darshan there is a major source of spiritual merit.
• The Ganga aarti (fire ceremony at the river at dawn and dusk) is a powerful collective act of worship that draws thousands of pilgrims daily.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per reason — 1 for identifying the reason, 2 for development, 3 for development with a specific Hindu belief or concept such as karma, moksha or darshan.]

practice_questions.text: 'Pilgrimage to a sacred place is the most important Hindu practice.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Pilgrimage to Varanasi and the river Ganges is among the most deeply embedded practices in popular Hinduism. Millions undertake pilgrimages each year, suggesting it holds central significance for many believers.
• The belief that dying in Varanasi guarantees moksha makes pilgrimage uniquely powerful: no other practice is believed to guarantee liberation with such certainty.
• The Kumbh Mela, the largest religious gathering on earth, demonstrates the enormous practical and emotional importance Hindus place on bathing at sacred sites during auspicious planetary alignments.
• Receiving darshan at a famous murti or sacred site is held to generate spiritual merit (punya) that accelerates progress toward moksha.

Arguments against:
• The Bhagavad Gita presents four margas — jnana, bhakti, karma and raja yoga — none of which requires pilgrimage to a specific place. A householder practising selfless service (sewa) may progress just as effectively.
• Many Hindu thinkers, including those in the Advaita Vedanta tradition, hold that Brahman is present everywhere equally. The medieval saint Tukaram and others taught that liberation is found in the purified heart, not at a sacred site.
• Home puja performed daily can be argued to be more important because it is sustained, everyday devotion rather than a once-in-a-lifetime journey. The Bhagavad Gita at XII 5 suggests that devotion in any form is accepted by God.
• Karma yoga, the path of selfless social action (sewa, dana), can be argued to be more important in the modern world: it transforms society rather than simply securing individual spiritual merit.

Mastering: Both sides developed with named sources and concepts (Bhagavad Gita XII 5; karma, moksha, punya; Varanasi; Tukaram); explicit weighing of arguments; a reasoned conclusion that justifies a position.
Secure: Two clear sides with some development; at least one named source or sacred site; a conclusion.
Developing: One side more developed; limited use of sources; partial conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; no or incorrect sources; no real conclusion.
[15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the role of a guru in Hindu worship and pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A guru is a spiritual teacher who guides disciples on the path to liberation through personal example and instruction.
• Receiving the darshan of a guru is considered a source of blessing and spiritual merit.
• Pilgrims often travel to a guru’s ashram (hermitage) as a form of pilgrimage, seeking guidance and transmission of spiritual energy.
• Sadhus (wandering ascetics) also provide darshan; their presence at sacred sites such as Varanasi enhances those sites’ spiritual power.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for some development; 3 marks for a developed answer that includes at least two aspects of the guru’s role.]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'exclusivism' in the context of religious dialogue.
practice_questions.marks: The belief that one's own religion is the only true path to salvation/ultimate truth (and that other religions cannot offer salvation/are false). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what ecumenism means.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that include: the movement seeking greater cooperation/understanding/unity among different Christian denominations (1 mark); reference to dialogue, shared worship or joint campaigns across denominations, e.g. Churches Together / World Council of Churches (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between exclusivism, inclusivism and pluralism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any of: exclusivism holds only one religion leads to salvation; inclusivism holds one religion is fullest/truest but others contain elements of truth; pluralism holds all major religions are equally valid paths. A fourth point could contrast the evangelical implications: exclusivism implies the importance of conversion; pluralism implies conversion is unnecessary. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why inter-faith dialogue is important in modern Britain.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Responses may include:
• Britain is one of the most religiously diverse societies in the world; dialogue reduces misunderstanding and prejudice between communities. Matthew 22:37–40 (love your neighbour) grounds this for Christians as a religious duty, not just a civic one.
• After events such as the 7/7 bombings or the Christchurch attacks, inter-faith dialogue is a tool for building resilience against extremism by creating relationships of trust between communities.
• John Hick's pluralist argument suggests that different religions encounter the same ultimate reality; dialogue can deepen each community's understanding of that reality.
• Many Christians believe the Great Commission (Matthew 28:18–20) requires honest dialogue as a form of witness, which can be done respectfully alongside genuine listening.
[6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 for identifying the reason, 2 for development, 3 for a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'Proselytisation and genuine inter-faith dialogue cannot coexist.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• If the aim of dialogue is ultimately to convert the other person, then it is not genuine dialogue but a form of persuasion. The other participant’s views are not taken seriously on their own terms.
• Religious minorities in Britain have historically experienced pressure to convert (e.g. colonial mission contexts); this history makes trust difficult when majority groups pursue outreach alongside dialogue.
• Pluralists such as John Hick argue that if all paths lead to the same reality, seeking to convert others is unnecessary and potentially arrogant.

Arguments against:
• Many Christians distinguish between witnessing (living out faith openly) and proselytising (using pressure or inducement). The Great Commission (Matthew 28:18–20) calls Christians to share the gospel — this can be done respectfully alongside genuine listening.
• Freedom of expression includes the freedom to share one’s beliefs and invite others to consider them. A society that bans persuasion restricts religious freedom.
• Exclusivist Christians, Muslims and others sincerely believe they possess truth that is important for others; concealing this belief in the name of dialogue would itself be dishonest.
• Many inter-faith practitioners say honest dialogue requires each party to bring their real convictions — including the belief that their tradition is true — provided they do not use manipulation or pressure.

Mastering (13–15 marks): Both sides fully developed with specific examples (Matthew 28:18–20, John Hick, freedom of expression); explicit weighing of arguments; justified conclusion on whether the two can coexist.
Secure (9–12 marks): Both sides explained with some development; at least one specific reference; conclusion reached.
Developing (5–8 marks): One side more developed; limited specific references; partial conclusion.
Emerging (1–4 marks): Brief, one-sided or largely descriptive. [15 marks including SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'pluralism' as a religious attitude.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that include: the view that all major world religions are equally valid (1 mark); paths to the same ultimate reality / salvation (1 mark). Reference to John Hick's analogy of different paths up the same mountain may be credited. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: State one belief Buddhists hold about what happens after death.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: consciousness is reborn in one of the six realms / kamma determines the nature of rebirth / the Bardo is an intermediate state between death and rebirth / death is governed by the principle of impermanence (anicca). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Bardo is in Tibetan Buddhist teaching.
practice_questions.marks: The Bardo is the intermediate state between death and rebirth [1]; it is a period (up to 49 days) during which the consciousness experiences visions, including a clear white light representing Buddha-nature, and has the opportunity to achieve liberation or take a new rebirth [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of the Tibetan Book of the Dead for Tibetan Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: the Tibetan Book of the Dead (Bardo Thodol) is a text read aloud by a lama to the dying and recently deceased [1]; it guides consciousness through the Bardo by describing the visions it will encounter and how to recognise them as projections of the mind [1]; its purpose is to help the consciousness achieve liberation by recognising the clear light of Buddha-nature rather than being drawn into an unfavourable rebirth [1]. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Buddhist beliefs about kamma and rebirth influence attitudes to death and mourning.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Kamma means that actions performed in life shape the conditions of the next rebirth — this leads Theravada communities to perform merit-transfer rituals (offering food to monks, donating to temples) on behalf of the deceased, with the belief that generated merit can benefit the dead. This reflects the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta's teaching that intentional action has consequences.
• Belief in the six realms of existence means that mourners may act to help the deceased achieve a favourable rebirth. In Tibetan Buddhism, the Bardo Thodol is read to help consciousness avoid the lower realms and ideally achieve liberation.
• Belief in impermanence (anicca) shapes the tone of mourning — clinging to the dead is seen as harmful since it is rooted in the delusion that things persist. The Dhammapada 170–171 teaches that one who sees the world as a bubble is not trapped by death's power.
[6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 simple point, 2 developed, 3 with teaching/source]

practice_questions.text: 'Buddhist death rituals are more about the living than the dead.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Merit-transfer rituals, chanting and offerings comfort the bereaved and reinforce community bonds, giving mourners a sense of purposeful action. The gathering of monks and community at a Theravada funeral serves to strengthen the lay sangha.
• The Obon festival in Japan is clearly a communal and social event, with family gatherings, dances and lanterns — it can be argued that remembering and honouring ancestors serves the psychological needs of the living as much as the dead.
• The emphasis in Buddhist teachings on impermanence is directed at the living: Dhammapada 170–171 uses death as a teaching tool to encourage the living to practise the Dhamma now.

Arguments against:
• Tibetan Buddhist practice is explicitly oriented towards helping the consciousness of the deceased navigate the Bardo. The Bardo Thodol is read to the dead, not the living, and its aim is to improve the deceased's rebirth or achieve their liberation.
• Theravada merit-transfer believes generated merit can genuinely influence the next life of the deceased — this is a sincere belief that the rituals benefit the dead, not merely the living.
• The six realms doctrine holds that beings in lower realms (hungry ghosts, hell realms) genuinely need help; practices aimed at transferring merit or guiding consciousness are understood as having real effects on the deceased.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with Theravada/Tibetan/Japanese comparison, named teachings (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Bardo Thodol, Dhammapada), explicit weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with some Buddhist content and teaching; conclusion offered.
Developing: One side stronger; some relevant Buddhist content; limited source references.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no Buddhist teaching. [15 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of Obon for Japanese Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Obon is a Japanese festival observed in mid-August in which it is believed the spirits of deceased ancestors return to visit the family home [1]; families clean graves, light lanterns to guide spirits back, place offerings before the home altar and perform traditional Obon dances [1]; the festival connects Buddhist beliefs about the realm of hungry ghosts and merit with Japanese ancestor veneration, showing the influence of local culture on Buddhist practice [1]. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what the term 'avatara' means in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: The incarnation or descent of a deity into a physical form in the material world. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Hindus mean by 'Saguna Brahman'.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Brahman understood with attributes or qualities; the personal God who can be known, loved and approached through worship; associated with deity forms such as Vishnu and Shiva; contrasted with Nirguna Brahman (without attributes). [2 marks — 1 for a simple statement, 2 for a more developed description]

practice_questions.text: Outline the role of Shakti in Hindu belief.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Shakti is the divine feminine energy or power; it activates and empowers the male deities of the Trimurti; without Shakti the universe could not function; the Tridevi (Saraswati, Lakshmi, Parvati/Durga) are the Shakti of the Trimurti; Shaktism is the tradition that regards the Goddess as the supreme divine reality. [3 marks — 1 for identifying Shakti as divine feminine energy, 2 for relating it to the Trimurti or Tridevi, 3 for a full account including the Shaktism tradition or the idea of divine action depending on Shakti]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Hindus understand the relationship between Brahman and the material world.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Saguna Brahman: Brahman as personal God (Bhagavan/Ishvara) who creates, sustains and judges; the Trimurti and avatara doctrine express how this personal God is actively engaged with the world.
• Nirguna Brahman: Brahman as beyond all attributes and form, not fully describable by any human concept; the Kena Upanishad (II 3) suggests Brahman is known precisely through acknowledging it cannot be known.
• Antaryami: Brahman as inner controller present within every being; Chandogya Upanishad 'Tat tvam asi' — 'That thou art' expresses Brahman's immanence.
• Maya: the material world is a real manifestation of Brahman's creative power but not the deepest reality.
[6 marks — 3 marks per way: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a developed explanation with a source]

practice_questions.text: 'The use of murti in worship shows that Hindus do not truly believe in one ultimate God.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments that could support the statement: Hinduism has a vast pantheon of deities each with distinct personalities; murti worship can appear polytheistic to outsiders; different communities worship Vishnu, Shiva or the Goddess with very different devotional approaches; some Hindu reform movements (Arya Samaj) have themselves criticised murti worship as inconsistent with Vedic monotheism.

Arguments that could challenge the statement: the Trimurti and Tridevi are expressions of one Brahman, not separate gods — the many divine forms are understood as windows onto one ultimate reality; the avatara doctrine (Bhagavad Gita context) presents Vishnu as one supreme personal God who descends in many forms; Saguna Brahman is the personal God (Bhagavan/Ishvara) while Nirguna Brahman is the impersonal absolute — both point to one reality; the murti is understood as a genuine presence of Brahman, not a separate deity; the Kena Upanishad (II 3) affirms one unknowable ultimate; 'Tat tvam asi' (Chandogya Upanishad) affirms the unity of all being.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Kena Upanishad I; Chandogya Upanishad; Bhagavad Gita context; Arya Samaj), explicit weighing of arguments and a justified conclusion.
Secure: two clear perspectives with some use of Hindu teaching; conclusion present.
Developing: one side more developed; some relevant content; limited source use.
Emerging: one-sided or very brief; little specific Hindu content.

practice_questions.text: Outline what Hindus believe about the concept of antaryami.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: antaryami means 'inner controller'; it refers to Brahman as present within the heart of every being; the Chandogya Upanishad expresses this as 'Tat tvam asi' ('That thou art'); the Katha Upanishad (I ii 20) describes the atman/Brahman as smaller than the smallest yet greater than the greatest; this means Brahman is not only transcendent but genuinely immanent within each person. [3 marks — 1 for defining antaryami, 2 for developing the idea with a textual reference, 3 for relating it to the broader understanding of Brahman as immanent]

practice_questions.text: State what event Ashura commemorates for Shi'a Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for: the martyrdom of Hussayn ibn Ali / the death of Hussayn at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE / the martyrdom of the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how Muslims celebrate Eid-ul-Fitr.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for any two of: communal prayer at the mosque or open space / wearing new or best clothes / giving gifts especially to children / sharing meals with family and friends / paying Zakat al-Fitr (special charitable payment before Eid prayer) / the festival marks the successful completion of Ramadan. [2 marks — 1 per valid point]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Muslims mean by 'Greater Jihad'.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for: Greater Jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) is the inner / spiritual struggle / against the lower self (nafs) / to resist sin, selfishness and moral failing / to live according to 'the straight path' (as-sirat al-mustaqim) / it is considered more important than Lesser Jihad / it involves promoting Ma'ruf (what is right) and resisting Munkar (what is wrong). Award three marks for a developed outline covering at least two of these elements. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two conditions that Islamic teaching places on Lesser Jihad.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Lesser Jihad must be defensive, not offensive. The Qur'an states: 'Fight in the cause of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress limits' (Surah 2:190). This means armed struggle is only permitted when the Muslim community is under attack.
• If the enemy seeks peace, Muslims must accept it. Surah 8:61 teaches: 'if they incline to peace, then incline to it also and put your trust in Allah.' This prevents Jihad from being used as a pretext for endless conflict.
• Lesser Jihad must be declared by legitimate authority and be a last resort when other means of resolving injustice have failed.
• Non-combatants and civilians must be protected — Islamic jurisprudence forbids harming the innocent.
Mastering: Two developed conditions, each supported by a named Qur'anic source, with clear explanation of significance.
Secure: Two conditions developed, at least one source.
Developing: Two conditions but limited development or no source.
Emerging: One condition, brief. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Greater Jihad is more important than Lesser Jihad for Muslims today.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• A widely-cited saying attributed to Muhammad describes him as telling his companions after a military campaign that they had returned from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle — the struggle against the self. Although this hadith is considered weak by many classical scholars, it shows that Islamic tradition has long placed Greater Jihad above Lesser.
• The inner spiritual struggle against sin, selfishness and moral weakness is relevant to every Muslim every day, whereas armed struggle is rarely applicable in most Muslims' lives.
• Greater Jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) — striving to promote Ma'ruf and resist Munkar within oneself — is the foundation of Muslim ethics and shapes daily behaviour continuously.
• In non-Muslim majority countries, Lesser Jihad in the military sense has no direct application for most Muslims; Greater Jihad is universally meaningful.

Arguments against:
• Lesser Jihad is listed as one of the Shi'a Ten Obligatory Acts and is therefore a formal religious duty, not simply optional.
• Some Muslim scholars argue that defending the oppressed and resisting injustice through legitimate means is an urgent communal obligation that cannot be postponed in favour of inner reflection alone.
• The Qur'an does specify conditions under which Lesser Jihad is obligatory (Surah 2:190), suggesting it cannot simply be set aside.
• What counts as 'more important' depends on context: in times of persecution or injustice, some scholars argue external struggle becomes the pressing duty.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed, named sources (hadith tradition, Surah 2:190, Surah 8:61), explicit comparison of individual and communal dimensions, explicit weighing and a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed, at least one source, clear conclusion.
Developing: Some engagement with both sides, limited sources or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided, brief, minimal sources. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the origin and significance of Eid-ul-Ghadeer for Shi'a Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for: Eid-ul-Ghadeer is celebrated on 18 Dhul Hijjah / it commemorates the event at Ghadir Khumm / where Shi'a Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad publicly appointed his cousin Ali as his rightful successor and Imam / it reflects the central Shi'a belief in the Imamate (the divinely guided leadership of Ali and his descendants) / it is not celebrated by Sunni Muslims who do not share this belief about Ali's appointment. Award three marks for a developed, accurate outline. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State one way in which believers think God might be revealed to human beings.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: through scripture / the Word of God; through Jesus Christ; through conscience; through miracles; through creation; through the life of inspirational people; through religious experience / worship / sacraments. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happened to Saul on the road to Damascus, according to Acts 9.
practice_questions.marks: Saul was struck down by a blinding light (1 mark); he heard the voice of Jesus asking why he was persecuting him, and was left blind for three days before emerging as a follower of Christ (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three different forms of religious experience that believers might have.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per form accurately identified and briefly described: conversion (a dramatic change of belief and life direction in response to a perceived encounter with God); mystical experience (a profound, often indescribable sense of union or contact with God or ultimate reality); charismatic/ecstatic experience (gifts of the Holy Spirit, including glossolalia, prophecy or healing in worship); visions (seeing or hearing God, Jesus or a heavenly figure); sacramental experience (encountering God through the Eucharist / Mass). [3 marks — up to 3 correct forms]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why some Christians consider religious experience to be evidence for God's existence.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per reason): 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a source. Example responses: (1) The conversion of Saul (Acts 9:1–6) involved a dramatic, unexpected encounter with the risen Jesus that transformed a persecutor into an apostle; the radical change in his life is seen as evidence that the experience was genuine and divine in origin. (2) The principle of credulity (Swinburne): if an experience seems real, it should be taken at face value; the widespread, cross-cultural nature of religious experience makes coincidence or mass delusion implausible; John 1:14 grounds this in the Christian belief that God actively reveals himself in the world. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Religious experiences are the strongest evidence for the existence of God.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Religious experiences are reported across all cultures and historical periods, giving them cross-cultural weight; the conversion of Saul (Acts 9:1–6) involved life-transforming consequences — unlikely to be explained as wish-fulfilment. The principle of credulity supports taking such experiences seriously. Sacramental experience (Mass / Holy Communion) provides ongoing access to divine encounter for millions. Mystical experiences carry the marks of noetic value, transience, passivity and ineffability identified by William James, suggesting they involve genuine contact with something beyond the self.

Arguments against: Psychological explanations (Freud: wish-fulfilment; the desire for a cosmic parent) and neurological explanations (temporal lobe activity) offer natural accounts of religious experience without needing God. The culturally-conditioned nature of experiences (Christians see Jesus; Muslims encounter Allah) suggests experiences reflect prior belief rather than objective reality. David Hume's scepticism about miracles extends to religious experiences: testimony is always weaker than the evidence for natural law. Even if the experience is genuine, it does not logically prove the God of any specific religion exists.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named thinkers and sources; explicit weighing (e.g. the cultural-conditioning argument vs the cumulative weight argument); justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with some development and at least one source; conclusion present.
Developing: Both sides attempted but unevenly; limited sources; weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; few sources; little to no conclusion. [15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Mass or Holy Communion can be considered a form of religious experience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per way): 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a source. Example responses: (1) Catholics believe that during the Eucharist the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation) — this means every Mass is an encounter with the risen Jesus, making it a form of direct religious experience of God's presence; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 grounds this in the words of Jesus at the Last Supper. (2) Even for Christians who do not hold transubstantiation, Communion is a sacramental act in which God's grace is understood to be genuinely communicated to believers; sharing bread and wine in the context of worship can produce feelings of peace, forgiveness and renewal that many describe in terms resembling mystical experience. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what Christians mean by 'agape'.
practice_questions.marks: Unconditional, self-giving love / the love God shows to humanity / the love Jesus commands Christians to show to others. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Christians believe about the ascension of Jesus.
practice_questions.marks: Jesus was taken up into heaven after his resurrection [1]; he promised to send the Holy Spirit and the disciples were told he would return in the same way [1]. [1 mark per valid point, max 2]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Christians believe about the incarnation of Jesus.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks from: God the Son took on human flesh in Jesus [1]; announced by the angel Gabriel to Mary in Luke 1:26-35 [1]; Jesus is both fully human and fully divine [1]; God entered human experience of suffering, grief and temptation [1].

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the resurrection is important for Christians.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- The resurrection proves Jesus is the Son of God and validates his teaching; Paul writes that without the resurrection faith is 'useless' (1 Corinthians 15). [up to 3 marks]
- The resurrection gives Christians hope that death is not the end; Matthew 28:1-10 shows Jesus risen, and Christians believe they will share in resurrection. [up to 3 marks]
- The resurrection demonstrates God's power over sin and death, confirming that atonement has been accomplished.
- Romans 6:23 links eternal life directly to Jesus, whose resurrection makes that life possible. [3 marks per point: 1 simple, 2 developed, 3 developed with source]

practice_questions.text: 'The crucifixion is more important than the resurrection for Christian belief.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- The crucifixion is the atoning act: Jesus pays the penalty for sin (Romans 3:24), making forgiveness possible.
- Romans 6:23 says 'the wages of sin is death' — the crucifixion is where that wage is paid on humanity's behalf.
- Mark 15:21-41 describes the tearing of the Temple curtain at Jesus's death, symbolising access to God restored.
- Some theologians argue the act of atonement is completed on the cross: 'It is finished' (John 19:30).

Arguments against / alternative views:
- Paul writes that without the resurrection 'your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15) — the resurrection confirms the crucifixion was not a defeat.
- The resurrection is the basis for Christian hope of life after death (Matthew 28:1-10).
- The ascension (Acts 1:9-11) follows the resurrection: without it, Jesus is not at the Father's right hand interceding for believers.
- Many Christians would say both are equally important: the death and resurrection together form one saving event that cannot be separated.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified personal conclusion about which is more important or whether they are inseparable.
Secure: Both sides present with at least one source; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources; conclusion present but not fully weighed.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; no real use of sources.

practice_questions.text: Describe the teaching of the Sermon on the Mount about Christian love.
practice_questions.marks: The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7) calls Christians to love even their enemies and to treat others as they wish to be treated [1]; it sets out the values of God's kingdom including mercy, peacemaking and generosity [1]. [1 mark per valid point, max 2]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'reconciliation'.
practice_questions.marks: The restoration of friendly relations between people or groups who have been in conflict. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of South Africa did.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying what it was (a body set up after apartheid to hear testimony from victims and perpetrators); one mark for describing its process or aim (perpetrators who confessed fully could apply for amnesty; it aimed at national healing and reconciliation rather than mass punishment). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian teachings about forgiveness.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct points, for example: Matthew 6:12 (the Lord's Prayer) teaches Christians to ask God to 'forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us'; Matthew 6:14 explicitly states that if we forgive others, God will also forgive us; Matthew 18:35 (the parable of the unmerciful servant) teaches that God's forgiveness is withdrawn from those who refuse to forgive others. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which religious teachings about justice differ from teachings about forgiveness.
practice_questions.marks: Credit two developed points, for example: Justice involves holding wrongdoers accountable and ensuring victims receive what they are owed — this may require punishment; forgiveness involves releasing resentment and choosing not to seek revenge even against someone who has not been punished, which can seem to conflict with justice (3 marks). The Hebrew prophets (e.g. Amos 5:21) stress that God demands righteous conduct and rejects empty worship in the absence of justice — but Jesus's teaching in Matthew 6:14 makes personal forgiveness a religious obligation regardless of whether the other person is punished; many religious thinkers therefore distinguish restorative justice (restoring relationships) from retributive justice (punishing wrongdoers) as a way of holding both together (3 marks). [6 marks — 3 marks per point: 1 basic, 2 developed, 3 developed with teaching]

practice_questions.text: 'It is never right to forgive without justice first.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Justice for victims requires that perpetrators face consequences for their actions; premature forgiveness can minimise the gravity of harm done and silence victims; Amos 5:21 shows that God takes justice seriously; without justice, reconciliation is built on a false peace that may break down; some theologians argue forgiveness without repentance from the wrongdoer does not require restoring a relationship.

Arguments against: Matthew 6:12-14 and 18:35 suggest Christians must forgive even when there is no justice; Jesus himself forgave those who crucified him without conditions; the TRC in South Africa offered amnesty (not full criminal justice) in exchange for truth, and Desmond Tutu argued this was the only way to achieve national healing; forgiveness liberates the victim from ongoing hatred; cycles of revenge show that justice without forgiveness often leads to more violence.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Matthew 6:14, Matthew 18:35, Amos 5:21, TRC/Tutu), explicit weighing and a justified conclusion engaging the tension between forgiveness and justice.
Secure: Both sides addressed with some scriptural support and a conclusion.
Developing: Some attempt at both sides; limited use of religious evidence.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no religious teaching cited. [15 marks + SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which religious believers work for social justice.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct points, for example: Religious organisations challenge unjust social systems through advocacy and campaigning (e.g. Martin Luther King Jr used his faith to oppose racial segregation); interfaith and community dialogue programmes help rebuild trust between groups in conflict; religious charities address root causes of injustice such as poverty and discrimination. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State the name of the Hindu festival that celebrates the victory of the devotee Prahlad over the demon Holika.
practice_questions.marks: Holi [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the Hindu festival of Diwali.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Diwali, the festival of lights, involves lighting rows of clay lamps (diyas), candles and electric lights to illuminate homes and public spaces.
• It celebrates the return of Rama and Sita to Ayodhya after Rama’s defeat of Ravana, as narrated in the Ramayana.
• Hindus worship the goddess Lakshmi for wealth and prosperity, and exchange sweets and gifts.
• Fireworks are set off as expressions of joy and to drive away evil.
[1 mark for a basic description; 2 marks for a developed description that includes either the story/meaning or two distinct practices.]

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which Hindu beliefs lead to actions that protect the environment.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Hindu belief that Brahman pervades all creation means that harming nature is spiritually wrong, not merely a practical concern. This motivates conservation efforts.
• The principle of ahimsa (non-violence) extends to animals, inspiring the protection of cows through goshallas (cow sanctuaries) and organisations like the Ahimsa Foundation for Cattle Protection.
• Hindu reverence for sacred rivers such as the Ganges motivates campaigns to protect them from pollution.
• The 1986 Assisi Declarations on Nature committed Hindu leaders to environmental stewardship rooted in religious teaching.
• Sewa International carries out environmental and community projects in line with the karma yoga principle of selfless service.
[1 mark for one basic point; 2 marks for two basic points or one developed point; 3 marks for two points that both link Hindu belief to specific environmental action.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Ganesh Chaturthi reflects important Hindu beliefs about the divine.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Ganesh Chaturthi celebrates the birthday of Ganesh, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati. The ten days of worship with clay images reflect the belief that deities can be made present in sacred images (murti) for the duration of a festival and then returned to their cosmic home through immersion.
