This reflects the belief in darshan — that contact with the divine presence in a murti brings blessing.
• The immersion of the clay Ganesh image at the end of the festival reflects Hindu beliefs about the cyclical nature of divine presence: the deity is welcomed, worshipped and then ceremonially released back into the cosmic waters, reflecting the Hindu understanding of creation and dissolution as eternal cycles.
• The worship of Ganesh as the remover of obstacles (Vighnaharta) and patron of beginnings reflects the Hindu belief that deities have specific powers that can be invoked through devotion. Beginning any enterprise with Ganesh puja reflects the bhakti path — seeking divine help through devotion.
• The social dimension of Ganesh Chaturthi — originally promoted by Bal Gangadhar Tilak as a community festival — reflects the belief that religion binds communities together and that shared worship expresses social solidarity.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per way — 1 for identifying the connection, 2 for developing the explanation, 3 for linking to a specific Hindu belief or concept.]

practice_questions.text: 'Hindu teachings about the environment are more important than Hindu teachings about social equality.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Hindu environmental ethics are deeply embedded in core beliefs: ahimsa (non-violence), the sacredness of creation and the principle that Brahman pervades all life make environmental care a fundamental spiritual duty.
• The 1986 Assisi Declarations on Nature gave formal religious authority to Hindu environmental commitment. Practical initiatives like goshallas and Sewa International show this being lived out on a large scale.
• The Mahabharata teaches that one who harms no creature attains moksha, giving environmental non-violence the highest possible spiritual weight.
• The river Ganges is worshipped as a goddess — environmental damage to her is literally an act of sacrilege, not merely a social problem.

Arguments against:
• Hindu teachings about social equality are arguably more urgently needed because human inequality causes immediate, preventable suffering. Gandhi saw challenging the caste system and ‘Untouchability’ as a core expression of karma yoga and ahimsa.
• The Bhagavad Gita’s teaching on spiritual equality — that all souls are equal before God regardless of birth — has radical implications for social justice. The Purusha Sukta presents society as one body, meaning social inequality harms the whole.
• The virtues of daya (compassion), dama (restraint) and kshama (patience) apply to human relationships as much as to the environment. A Hindu who practises daya must respond to human poverty and discrimination.
• Sewa International’s work spans both environmental projects and social welfare, suggesting that in practice Hindu ethics do not separate these concerns.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita XVI 1-3; Mahabharata; Assisi Declarations; Gandhi; goshallas; Sewa International); explicit weighing of the two forms of ethical concern; a justified conclusion.
Secure: Two sides with development; at least one named source per side; a conclusion that takes a position.
Developing: One side stronger; limited source use; partial conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided; no or incorrect sources; no real conclusion.
[15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning of Navaratri and its importance for Hindu worshippers.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Navaratri means ‘nine nights’; it honours the goddess Durga and her nine forms (Navadurga), celebrating the divine feminine power (Shakti).
• The festival commemorates Durga’s victory over the buffalo demon Mahishasura.
• In Gujarat, celebrants perform garba and dandiya raas dances; in Bengal, large clay Durga images are worshipped and then immersed.
• The tenth day (Vijaya Dashami/Dussehra) links Navaratri to the Ramayana through the burning of Ravana effigies.
• For worshippers, Navaratri affirms the power of the goddess and the importance of the divine feminine in Hindu life.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for some development; 3 marks for a developed answer that includes the story, practice and significance.]

practice_questions.text: State what the Pali word 'nirodha' means.
practice_questions.marks: Cessation / stopping / the ending of suffering. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the meaning of Nibbana in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: Nibbana literally means 'to extinguish' or 'to blow out'; it is the Buddhist term for the ultimate goal—the state reached when craving and the three poisons are completely extinguished and the cycle of rebirth ends. 1 mark: identifying Nibbana as the goal of Buddhism. 2 marks: explaining the literal meaning ('to extinguish') and linking it to the cessation of craving/the three poisons. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Threefold Way and explain how it organises the Noble Eightfold Path.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per category of the Threefold Way, each requiring the name and the relevant path factors:
• Sila (ethical conduct)—Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood.
• Samadhi (meditation)—Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration.
• Panna (wisdom)—Right View, Right Intention.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the importance of the Noble Eightfold Path for Buddhists.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Eightfold Path is the Fourth Noble Truth and represents the practical way to end suffering (dukkha) by overcoming craving (tanha) and the three poisons.
• The Magga-vibhanga Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 45:8) defines each factor, confirming the path's authority in early Buddhist teaching.
• The path constitutes the Middle Way between sensory indulgence and harsh asceticism, avoiding the extremes the Buddha himself had tried and rejected.
• The grouping into the Threefold Way (sila, samadhi, panna) shows how ethics supports meditation and meditation supports wisdom, with each dimension reinforcing the others.
• The Dhammapada (1–2) teaches that all experience is shaped by mind, underpinning the importance of Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration.
• For Theravada practitioners, following the path leads to becoming an Arahant; for Mahayana practitioners, it underpins the Bodhisattva ideal.
Mastering: the path's importance is explained with named references, its structure is analysed and denominational differences are addressed.
Secure: the path's importance explained with a named reference and some development.
Developing: basic description of the path's role with limited development.
Emerging: simple mention of the path without explanation. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The Third Noble Truth is the most important of the Four Noble Truths.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Without the Third Noble Truth's declaration that suffering can end (nirodha), the first two truths would be purely diagnostic with no hope of cure. Nibbana as the goal gives the entire Buddhist system its purpose and direction.
• The literal meaning of Nibbana ('to extinguish') provides a concrete, achievable aim; the Udana (8:3) confirms its reality as 'the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned.'
• Without the prospect of Nibbana, the Eightfold Path (the Fourth Noble Truth) would have nothing to aim at. The Third Noble Truth therefore logically grounds the Fourth.
• The Buddha's own attainment of Nibbana under the Bodhi tree proves that liberation is possible, making the Third Noble Truth the most inspiring and hope-giving of the four.

Arguments against or offering a different priority:
• The First Noble Truth (Dukkha) could be argued as most important because without honestly recognising suffering, no one would be motivated to seek the path. Honest diagnosis is the precondition for everything that follows.
• The Fourth Noble Truth (Magga) could be prioritised on practical grounds: without the Eightfold Path, the possibility of ending suffering is just an idea. The path makes liberation practically achievable.
• The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11) presents all four truths as an integrated whole; later Buddhist teachers have often warned against elevating one truth above the others.
• For Mahayana Buddhists, the Bodhisattva ideal reframes the goal: seeking Nibbana for oneself alone is less important than the compassionate aim of helping all beings reach liberation. This suggests the Third Noble Truth (personal liberation) may need to be supplemented or even transcended.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources, explicit weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered with at least one named source and a clear conclusion.
Developing: some argument on each side with limited sources.
Emerging: one-sided response with no sources. [15 marks, SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the role of Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration within the Threefold Way.
practice_questions.marks: Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration both belong to the Samadhi (meditation) category of the Threefold Way. Right Mindfulness means maintaining present-moment awareness of body, feelings, mind and mental objects. Right Concentration means developing deep meditative states (jhana) that unify and calm the mind. Together, they train the mind so that wisdom (panna) can arise. 1 mark: placing both in the Samadhi category. 1 mark: explaining Right Mindfulness. 1 mark: explaining Right Concentration. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what Christians mean by the term 'mission'.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: the calling of the Church to go into the world and share the Gospel (1); the Church's responsibility to make disciples of all nations (1); serving others as an expression of Christian love and obedience (1). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Taize community does.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Points may include: it is a monastic community in France (1); it draws young people for prayer, Bible study and community life (1); it is known for simple repeated chants used in worship (1); it works for reconciliation between divided Christians (1); it was founded by Brother Roger Schutz in 1940 (1). Maximum 2 marks. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the World Council of Churches promotes Christian unity.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per valid way up to 3. Points may include: it brings over 350 denominations together for dialogue (1); it works for peace and justice on global issues (1); it advocates for human rights and creation care (1); it promotes reconciliation between divided churches (1); it encourages joint worship and mission across denominations (1). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why supporting the persecuted Church is important for Christians.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks per reason. Points may include:
• Christians are commanded to love one another as Jesus loved them (John 13:34-35) — this love crosses national and denominational lines, requiring practical action to support those imprisoned or harmed for their faith (3).
• Matthew 25:31-46 teaches that serving those who suffer is serving Christ himself — so supporting persecuted Christians is an act of obedience to Jesus's teaching about the final judgement (3).
• The Church is one body (1 Corinthians 12) — when one part suffers, all suffer — so supporting the persecuted is an expression of Christian solidarity (2). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Evangelism should be the Church's top priority in the 21st century.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation presenting the case for verbal proclamation (Great Commission Matthew 28:16-20; Romans 1:16; Acts 1:8; John 14:6 — Jesus as the only way) alongside the case for social action and a holistic mission (Matthew 25:31-46; Mark 12:31; Christian Aid's work; Iona/Corrymeela as mission through presence). Considers new forms of church as an expression of evangelism adapted to modern life. Justified conclusion that weighs which approach best reflects the whole Gospel. [13-15 marks]
Secure: Two developed arguments on each side, some use of scripture or named organisations, conclusion present but not fully weighed. [9-12 marks]
Developing: Some relevant content; one side better developed; limited use of scripture or examples. [5-8 marks]
Emerging: Brief, undeveloped points; little or no reference to Christian teaching. [1-4 marks]
SPaG assessed on this question.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which ecumenical communities contribute to Christian mission.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks per way. Points may include:
• Corrymeela brought Catholics and Protestants together in Northern Ireland during the Troubles, showing that the peace Christ offers transcends historical divisions — embodying John 13:34-35 ('love one another') in a divided society (3).
• Taize draws thousands of young people into encounter with Christ through communal prayer and simple worship — acting as a form of mission that draws people who might not attend a traditional church (3).
• Iona's commitment to justice and peace reflects the understanding that mission includes advocacy for the marginalised, grounded in the prophetic tradition and Matthew 25:31-46 (3).
• The World Council of Churches coordinates mission across 350 denominations, enabling a unified Christian voice on global justice issues (2). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what agnosticism means.
practice_questions.marks: The view that the existence of God is unknown and perhaps unknowable; neither affirming nor denying God's existence. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what humanism is.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that include: a non-religious worldview (1 mark) based on reason and/or empathy / human dignity / the view that humans can live ethical lives without supernatural belief (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three values that religious and non-religious people share.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each (up to 3) for any of: human dignity; compassion/care for the vulnerable; freedom of conscience/belief; honesty and fairness; concern to reduce suffering; support for human rights; commitment to helping those in need; opposition to injustice. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why dialogue between religious and non-religious people is significant for society.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Responses may include:
• Dialogue reduces prejudice and builds mutual understanding in an increasingly non-religious society; the 2021 census shows over 37% of people in England and Wales have no religion, so religious communities must engage rather than ignore this. Matthew 22:37–40 ('love your neighbour') includes non-religious neighbours.
• Shared values (human dignity, compassion, care for the vulnerable) provide a foundation for working together on social issues such as poverty, homelessness, and environmental action. Humanists UK and many faith organisations already collaborate on such causes.
• If religious voices are excluded from public debate on the grounds that they are 'not secular,' a large proportion of society loses its voice. The Tony Blair Foundation argues that secular governments need to engage with religious communities, not dismiss them.
• Dialogue can correct misunderstandings: many religious people mischaracterise atheism as nihilism (no values), and many atheists mischaracterise religion as blind faith. Genuine dialogue replaces caricatures with accurate understanding.
[6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 for identifying the reason, 2 for development, 3 for a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'Secular values should take precedence over religious values in a modern society.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• In a society with diverse religious and non-religious views, only values grounded in reason and the common good (secular values) can be applied to everyone without imposing one religion on others. Demanding religious compliance from non-believers restricts their freedom of conscience.
• The National Secular Society argues that a neutral state — one that privileges no religion — best protects religious freedom for all, including minorities.
• Secular ethics, grounded in evidence and empathy (as Humanists UK argues), can adapt to new knowledge (e.g. medical discoveries about consciousness, embryo development) in ways that religiously fixed doctrines often cannot.
• Laws based on specific religious teachings (e.g. restricting divorce or same-sex relationships) impose a particular theology on citizens who do not share it.

Arguments against:
• Religious communities also constitute part of 'the public.' Their values have as much democratic legitimacy as secular ones and should not automatically be subordinated. Matthew 22:37–40 generates practical ethical commitments (care for the poor, welcome for the stranger) that have shaped British social policy for centuries.
• The claim that secular reason is neutral is itself contested: secular values reflect particular philosophical traditions (Enlightenment liberalism) that are not universally shared. Humanist ethics, grounded in empathy and reason, is a substantive worldview, not a neutral default.
• Many human rights were championed by religious believers (William Wilberforce on abolition, Martin Luther King on civil rights). Marginalising religious voices could impoverish rather than enrich public ethical debate.
• The Tony Blair Foundation argues that ignoring religion in global affairs leads to policy failures; the same argument applies domestically.

Mastering (13–15 marks): Both sides fully developed; named references (National Secular Society, Humanists UK, Tony Blair Foundation, Matthew 22:37–40); explicit weighing of arguments; justified conclusion addressing whether secular values should take precedence.
Secure (9–12 marks): Both sides explained with some development; at least one specific reference; conclusion reached.
Developing (5–8 marks): One side more developed; limited specific references; partial conclusion.
Emerging (1–4 marks): Brief, one-sided or largely descriptive. [15 marks including SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by secularism as a political principle.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that include: the principle that the state should be neutral on religion / no religion should have special privilege (1 mark); religious law should not be imposed on non-believers / all citizens should be treated equally regardless of religion or non-belief (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: State the Arabic term for the concept of prophethood in Islam.
practice_questions.marks: Risalah. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the angel Jibril in Islamic belief.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: Jibril is the chief angel in Islam (1 mark) who was responsible for conveying Allah's revelation to the prophets, including delivering the Qur'an word by word to Muhammad (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline Muslim beliefs about the role and importance of the holy books (Kutub).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks: Allah revealed scriptures to various prophets throughout history (1 mark); these include the Tawrat (Moses), Zabur (David), Injil (Jesus) and the Qur'an (Muhammad) (1 mark); Muslims believe previous scriptures became distorted over time, while the Qur'an is the final, perfectly preserved message from Allah (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muhammad is considered to hold a special position among the prophets in Islamic belief.
practice_questions.marks: Possible points: Muhammad is described as the 'seal of the prophets' (Khatam an-Nabiyyin) — meaning he is the last and final prophet, closing the line of prophethood (1+1 mark). The Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad as the final, undistorted and perfectly preserved scripture, making his message authoritative for all time (1+1 mark). Surah al-Imran (3:144) places Muhammad within the line of prophets while also indicating his unique role as the culmination of prophethood (1+1 mark). Surah al-Alaq (Surah 96) records the first revelation to Muhammad, marking the beginning of a new era of divine guidance (1+1 mark). [6 marks: 3 marks per reason — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'All prophets in Islam are equally important.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: All prophets receive their message from the same Allah and convey the same essential monotheistic message; the Qur'an says messengers were sent to every community; each prophet served a vital role in his time and context; Islam forbids making distinctions that dishonour any prophet. Arguments against: The Qur'an (3:144) identifies Muhammad as the final messenger, giving him unique finality; Ibrahim is called the 'father of the prophets' and a hanif; Isa is described as performing miracles by divine permission; the Qur'an itself mentions that some prophets were given preference over others; the revealed book of each messenger had different scope and duration. Mastering: Both sides developed with named prophets, specific roles (khalifa, hanif, seal), sources (Surah 3:144, Surah 96, Surah 5:46), explicit weighing, and justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with sourcing; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or limited. Emerging: Brief, unsupported. [15 marks: SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: State the role of the angel Israfil on the Day of Judgement.
practice_questions.marks: Israfil will blow the trumpet to signal the resurrection of all souls on the Day of Judgement. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the Hebrew term for the Jewish principle that preserving life overrides other commandments.
practice_questions.marks: Pikuach Nefesh [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between positive commandments (aseh) and negative commandments (ta'ashe) in Jewish law.
practice_questions.marks: Positive commandments (aseh) are obligations to perform a specific action, such as lighting Shabbat candles or giving charity [1 mark]; negative commandments (ta'ashe) are prohibitions against performing certain actions, such as eating blood or committing theft [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Jews mean by 'ethical Mitzvot' and 'ritual Mitzvot'.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Ethical Mitzvot govern relationships between people, such as honesty, charity and care for the vulnerable (1 mark); ritual Mitzvot govern the relationship between a Jew and G-d, such as prayer, Shabbat and dietary laws (1 mark); both types are considered binding obligations from G-d rather than suggestions (1 mark); the two are interconnected — ethical and religious practice reinforce each other in Jewish thought (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the principle of Pikuach Nefesh affects Jewish life and practice.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Pikuach Nefesh allows (and requires) breaking Shabbat restrictions to save a life: a Jewish doctor must travel and work on Shabbat if a patient’s life is at risk, because the Torah principle of saving life (derived from Leviticus 19:16 — “do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbour”) takes precedence.
• Pikuach Nefesh permits an ill person to eat non-kosher food if that is the only food available to sustain their health, showing that dietary laws (important as they are) do not rank above preserving life.
• Pikuach Nefesh shows the Jewish belief that human life has supreme sanctity — rooted in Genesis 1:27 (humans created in G-d’s image) — and that preserving it is G-d’s will even when it requires temporary suspension of other commandments.
• Only three commandments cannot be overridden even to save a life: murder, sexual immorality and idol worship — showing that some moral absolutes remain even within the principle of Pikuach Nefesh.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per way — 1 for naming, 2 for explaining, 3 for developing with a source]

practice_questions.text: 'The ethical Mitzvot are more important than the ritual Mitzvot for Jewish life today.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Ethical Mitzvot (justice, charity, honesty) have universal moral value and shape how Jews relate to society; they are relevant in every context regardless of time or place.
• Progressive Jews emphasise ethical Mitzvot as the core of Torah, interpreting ritual Mitzvot as optional cultural expressions rather than binding divine commands.
• Pikuach Nefesh shows that even ritual commandments (like Shabbat) can be suspended for ethical reasons — suggesting ethics have a higher priority.
• Deuteronomy 30:19 (“choose life”) focuses on the moral dimension of choice rather than ritual practice.

Arguments against:
• Orthodox Jews regard all 613 Mitzvot as equally binding divine commands — there is no hierarchy between ethical and ritual obligations.
• Ritual Mitzvot (Shabbat, prayer, dietary laws) sustain Jewish identity, community cohesion and continuity across generations in a way that ethical principles alone cannot.
• Deuteronomy 11:18–21 and Numbers 15:37–41 command ritual practices (tefillin, tzitzit) as essential reminders of the covenant — not secondary to ethics.
• The Talmud consistently treats ritual and ethical Mitzvot as equally obligatory — both are expressions of love for G-d and other people.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Deuteronomy 30:19; Leviticus 19:16; Numbers 15:37–41; Pikuach Nefesh), explicit weighing of which argument is stronger, justified conclusion that recognises the interdependence of ethical and ritual Mitzvot.
Secure: Clear two-sided argument with some source reference; reasoned conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; limited source reference; simple conclusion.
Emerging: Only one perspective; no sources; minimal conclusion.
[15 marks — SPaG assessed on this response]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Jews believe about Divine Providence and free will.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Divine Providence means G-d guides and oversees the world and human history (1 mark); the Book of Jonah illustrates G-d guiding events to fulfil a divine purpose (1 mark); Judaism also affirms that humans have genuine free will — the Mitzvot only make sense if people can genuinely choose to obey or disobey (1 mark); Deuteronomy 30:19 (“choose life”) is a direct call to exercise free will (1 mark); thinkers like Maimonides argued G-d’s foreknowledge does not cancel human freedom (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Give one example of embedded inequality in a religious context.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: the male-only Catholic priesthood; restrictions on women preaching in some denominations; different dress codes for men and women; historical exclusion of women from religious leadership. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Truth and Reconciliation Commission sought to achieve.
practice_questions.marks: Credit any two developed points: it was chaired by Archbishop Tutu in post-apartheid South Africa (1996); it allowed perpetrators to confess in exchange for amnesty; victims could share their testimonies; it pursued restorative rather than punitive justice; it aimed at national healing and reconciliation. [1 mark per point, 2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Christians believe about gender equality, referring to at least two teachings.
practice_questions.marks: Credit three developed points. Examples: Genesis 1:27 teaches both male and female are made in God's image, establishing equal dignity; Galatians 3:28 declares there is neither male nor female in Christ; Acts 10:34-35 confirms God shows no favouritism; James 2:8-9 condemns discrimination; some Christians additionally hold that equality of dignity is compatible with complementary roles (Ephesians 5). [1 mark per point, 3 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the relationship between religion and culture affects attitudes to gender equality.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Credit two well-developed points. Examples: In some contexts, religion has reinforced cultural hierarchies — e.g. 1 Timothy 2:11-14 has been used to exclude women from leadership, reflecting the cultural norms of first-century Ephesus, though scholars debate whether this is a universal principle. In other contexts, religion has challenged cultural inequalities — Archbishop Tutu used Christian theology (John 13:34) and ubuntu to challenge the apartheid system, demonstrating that religious teaching can be a force for justice. [3 marks per point: 1 simple, 2 developed, 3 developed with source]

practice_questions.text: 'Religious teachings have done more harm than good in the fight for gender equality.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (statement is true):
- Passages such as 1 Timothy 2:11-14 and 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 have been used historically to exclude women from leadership and public roles.
- The male-only Catholic priesthood is an embedded inequality that some argue conflicts with the equal dignity asserted in Genesis 1:27.
- Religious institutions have sometimes reinforced cultural norms of female subordination rather than challenging them.
- Non-religious/humanist arguments for gender equality do not depend on religious premises and may be more consistent and universal.

Arguments against (statement is false):
- Genesis 1:27 and Galatians 3:28 provide strong theological foundations for gender equality that have inspired egalitarian Christian movements.
- Archbishop Tutu's work on the TRC drew on Christian theology of equality and reconciliation to challenge systemic racial injustice — a model applicable to gender justice too.
- The abolitionist movement, women's suffrage movement, and civil rights movement all drew on religious motivation.
- James 2:8-9 explicitly condemns favouritism; John 13:34 commands love without distinction.
- Many denominations now ordain women at all levels of ministry and have been at the forefront of gender equality campaigns.

Mastering: Both sides argued with developed reasoning; named sources (Genesis 1:27, Galatians 3:28, Archbishop Tutu/TRC); non-religious perspective included; explicit weighing; a justified and reasoned conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with some development; at least one named source; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some arguments from both sides; limited sources; brief or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or minimal; no sources; no real conclusion. [15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Explain two non-religious arguments for gender equality.
practice_questions.marks: Credit two well-developed points. Examples: Humanist ethics argues that equality is grounded in the equal capacity of all persons to experience wellbeing and suffering — there is no morally relevant difference between men and women that justifies unequal treatment. Feminist ethics holds that gender discrimination causes real harm to women's flourishing, careers and self-determination; the harm principle requires that society remove such barriers regardless of their religious justification. [3 marks per point: 1 simple, 2 developed, 3 developed with elaborated reasoning or example]

practice_questions.text: State the meaning of the term 'Kosher'.
practice_questions.marks: Food that is permitted under Jewish dietary law; fit or proper. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the Mohel at a Brit Milah ceremony.
practice_questions.marks: The Mohel is a trained Jewish professional [1] who performs the ritual circumcision on the eighth day of the baby boy's life [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the key features of a Jewish marriage ceremony.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: the ceremony takes place under the Huppah (wedding canopy) symbolising the couple's new home; a Ketubah (marriage contract) is signed before the ceremony; seven blessings (Sheva Brachot) are recited; the groom places a ring on the bride's finger; the groom breaks a glass at the end to recall the destruction of the Temple. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which attitudes towards Jewish dietary laws differ between Orthodox and Reform Jews.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Orthodox Jews follow all aspects of kashrut as binding commandments derived from Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14: they maintain two sets of kitchen equipment, wait between eating meat and dairy, and buy only certified kosher produce. They see dietary law as a discipline sanctifying daily life.
• Many Reform Jews do not observe the full kashrut laws, arguing that the spiritual and ethical principles of Judaism matter more than ancient food regulations. Some avoid pork and shellfish but do not separate meat and milk. Reform Judaism emphasises underlying values such as reducing animal suffering.
• Both groups agree that the underlying purpose of dietary laws is to cultivate mindfulness and holiness in everyday life, but they interpret how strictly this must be applied today.
[6 marks — 3 marks per difference: 1 for a simple statement, 2 for development, 3 for a relevant source of wisdom]

practice_questions.text: 'Brit Milah is the most important Jewish rite of passage.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Brit Milah is the physical sign of the covenant between G-d and Abraham (Genesis 17:9-12), the foundational relationship of Judaism; without it, a male Jew is considered to have broken the covenant.
• It takes place on the eighth day of life, making it the first religious act performed for a Jewish male — prior even to the child having any conscious identity.
• The presence of the metaphorical Chair of Elijah and the naming of the child make it a decisive moment of entry into Jewish identity and community.

Arguments against:
• Bar Mitzvah arguably marks the more significant moment: the child becomes personally responsible for the Mitzvot and takes on adult religious obligations. It is the moment chosen by the individual, not performed on them as infants.
• Yom Kippur (atonement) and Shabbat affect every Jew every week or year; Brit Milah applies only to males and only once.
• Marriage (Kiddushin) is described as the foundation of Jewish family life; Genesis 2:24 calls the married couple 'one flesh'. Without marriage, Jewish continuity and community life would be impossible.
• Burial and the Kaddish connect Jews to belief in resurrection and G-d's ongoing presence even in death, making them profoundly significant to the entire community.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Genesis 17:9-12, Genesis 2:24, Leviticus, the Mitzvot), comparison of male and female rites of passage, Orthodox vs Reform differences noted, and a justified conclusion identifying which rite is most fundamental and why.
Secure: Clear arguments for and against with relevant sources and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points on both sides but sources limited or not developed; conclusion present but not fully argued.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no use of sources. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of the Kaddish prayer in Jewish mourning.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: the Kaddish is an Aramaic prayer of praise to G-d, recited by mourners at the graveside and during services for eleven months after bereavement; it does not mention death or grief but focuses entirely on praising G-d, showing faith even in loss; reciting it requires a minyan (quorum of ten) and connects the individual mourner to the wider Jewish community; it affirms the ongoing relationship between G-d and the Jewish people even in times of suffering. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

practice_questions.text: State what 'Gan Eden' means in Jewish belief.
practice_questions.marks: The Garden of Eden / paradise where righteous souls rest after death in G-d's presence [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Jews believe about the relationship between the soul and the body.
practice_questions.marks: Judaism teaches that a human being is a unity of soul and body [1 mark]; the soul (neshama) is the divine element given by G-d at creation (Genesis 2:7 — G-d breathed life into humanity), while the body is its earthly dwelling, both of which are valued and respected [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Jews believe about life after death, referring to Sheol, Gan Eden and Gehenna.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Sheol is the shadowy realm of the dead in the Hebrew Bible, understood as a diminished state rather than reward or punishment (1 mark); Gan Eden is paradise where the souls of the righteous rest in G-d’s presence after death (1 mark); Gehenna is a place of purification for souls, generally not permanent — most Jewish traditions say souls remain there no more than twelve months (1 mark); Daniel 12:2–3 describes a future resurrection and different destinies for the righteous and the wicked (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish teachings about the sanctity of life.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• All humans are created in the image of G-d (Genesis 1:27 — tzelem Elohim): this gives every person intrinsic worth and dignity, regardless of age, ability or status. This means human life cannot be treated as expendable.
• G-d breathed life directly into humanity (Genesis 2:7): life is a divine gift and therefore belongs ultimately to G-d, not to humans. This shapes Jewish opposition to taking life without divine sanction.
• The commandment “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13) makes the protection of life a direct divine obligation.
• Pikuach Nefesh (Leviticus 19:16) — the duty to preserve life — overrides almost all other Mitzvot, showing how highly Judaism values life: saving a life on Shabbat, for example, is not just permitted but required.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per teaching — 1 for naming, 2 for explaining, 3 for developing with a source]

practice_questions.text: 'Jewish beliefs about life after death are less important than Jewish beliefs about how to live in this world.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Judaism is often described as a ‘this-world’ religion: the Torah is primarily concerned with how Jews live in the present — keeping the Mitzvot, building a just society, observing the covenant.
• The 613 Mitzvot deal overwhelmingly with life in this world; Jewish law (‘halachah’) is a detailed guide to living, not primarily a preparation for death.
• Deuteronomy 30:19 (“choose life”) focuses on present choices; Pikuach Nefesh prioritises life in this world above ritual observance.
• Progressive (Reform) Jews often interpret afterlife language metaphorically, suggesting that what matters is living according to Jewish values now.

Arguments against:
• Orthodox Judaism includes belief in bodily resurrection (tekhiyat ha-metim) as one of Maimonides’ thirteen principles of faith — it is a core doctrinal belief, not optional.
• The themes of Rosh Hashannah and Yom Kippur — G-d’s judgement, the Book of Life — show that life after death is deeply embedded in Jewish prayer and community life.
• Daniel 12:2–3 gives clear scriptural basis for resurrection and future judgement, showing that afterlife belief is not peripheral but rooted in scripture.
• The hope of Gan Eden (paradise) gives meaning and comfort to Jews facing suffering, persecution or death — as evidenced throughout Jewish history.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Deuteronomy 30:19; Daniel 12:2–3; Genesis 1:27; Maimonides’ principles), explicit weighing, justified conclusion that may acknowledge the balance between this-worldly ethics and afterlife belief in Judaism.
Secure: Clear two-sided argument with some source reference; reasoned conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; limited source reference; simple conclusion.
Emerging: Only one perspective; no sources; minimal conclusion.
[15 marks — SPaG assessed on this response]

practice_questions.text: Outline how Jewish views on resurrection and the afterlife differ between Orthodox and Progressive communities.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Orthodox Judaism affirms bodily resurrection (tekhiyat ha-metim) as a core belief, listed in Maimonides’ thirteen principles (1 mark); at the end of time, the dead will be physically raised and face G-d’s judgement (1 mark); Progressive Jews often focus on the immortality of the soul rather than bodily resurrection (1 mark); some Progressive Jews interpret afterlife language metaphorically — meaning a person’s influence and legacy live on (1 mark); Conservative Jews generally retain traditional language but allow a range of interpretations (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what Christians mean by the 'Parousia'.
practice_questions.marks: The Second Coming / the expected return of Jesus Christ at the end of history / Christ coming again to judge the living and the dead. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Catholics believe about purgatory.
practice_questions.marks: Purgatory is a state of purification after death [1] in which souls are cleansed of the effects of sin in preparation for entering heaven [1]. [1 mark per valid point, max 2]

practice_questions.text: Outline two Christian beliefs about heaven.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks from: heaven is being in God's presence in joy and peace [1]; Jesus speaks of 'many rooms' in his Father's house (John 14:1-3) [1]; heaven involves full knowledge of and communion with God [1]; the creeds describe it as 'everlasting life' [1].

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why resurrection is important for Christian belief about life after death.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Resurrection confirms that death is not the end; Paul argues in 1 Corinthians 15:17 that without resurrection 'your faith is futile', making it foundational to all Christian hope. [up to 3 marks]
- The resurrection of Christ is the model and guarantee of believers' own resurrection; Paul uses the image of a seed to show the body is 'sown perishable' but raised 'imperishable' (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). [up to 3 marks]
- Belief in resurrection shapes how Christians face death and grief; they do not mourn 'like the rest, who have no hope.' [3 marks per point: 1 simple, 2 developed, 3 developed with source]

practice_questions.text: 'Belief in hell is not compatible with belief in a loving God.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- If God is benevolent (all-loving), it seems contradictory to allow any person to suffer eternally.
- Universalists argue that a truly loving God would ultimately reconcile all people to himself.
- Some argue annihilationism (the wicked simply cease to exist) is more compatible with love than eternal torment.
- Matthew 5:29-30's dramatic language may be hyperbolic, not literal.

Arguments against / alternative views:
- Christians argue hell is the consequence of a person's own choice to reject God; a loving God does not force people into relationship. Free Will requires the possibility of permanent rejection.
- Matthew 25:31-46 shows Jesus teaching that judgement is real and has eternal consequences; this is part of Jesus's own teaching, not a later addition.
- The Nicene Creed affirms Christ 'will come again to judge the living and the dead' — judgement, not universalism, is the creedal position.
- Hell may be understood as the absence of God rather than active punishment; the loss of divine love is its own torment.
- Some denominations (annihilationists) hold a view of hell compatible with love: the wicked cease to exist rather than suffer forever.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Matthew 25:31-46, Matthew 5:29-30, 1 Corinthians 15); explicit weighing of competing views; justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with at least one source; comparison made; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources; conclusion present but not fully weighed.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; little or no use of sources; no justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which belief in the Second Coming (Parousia) affects how Christians live.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: Christians live with urgency, as if Jesus could return at any time [1]; they work for justice and care for the poor as Matthew 25:31-46 shows judgement is based on how they treated others [1]; they hold their possessions lightly, not placing ultimate value on earthly things [1]; they find comfort in suffering, knowing God will ultimately right all wrongs [1]. [1 mark per valid point, max 2]

practice_questions.text: State what Muslims mean by 'Barzakh'.
practice_questions.marks: Barzakh is the intermediate state / period between death and the Day of Judgement. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Islamic belief in Akhirah.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: Akhirah is the Islamic concept of the afterlife — the eternal existence that follows death and the Day of Judgement (1 mark); Muslims believe that this life is a preparation for Akhirah, where each soul will be judged by Allah for their deeds and sent to either al-Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell) (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline two different Muslim views on the relationship between predestination (al-Qadr) and human free will.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks: the Mu'tazilite school strongly emphasised human free will, arguing that predestination without freedom would make divine punishment unjust (1 mark); the Al-Ash'ari school held that Allah's foreknowledge and power encompass all events, but that humans 'acquire' responsibility for their choices (1 mark); most Muslims accept that both divine foreknowledge and human accountability are true simultaneously, with the precise relationship remaining a mystery (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the belief in Akhirah might affect the life of a Muslim today.
practice_questions.marks: Possible points: Belief in Akhirah encourages Muslims to live ethically because every action is recorded and will be judged — the Qur'an (2:155) describes this life as a test, motivating perseverance and moral seriousness (1+1 mark). The belief in al-Jannah and Jahannam as real consequences provides motivation to pray, give to charity and avoid serious sin — not merely out of social pressure but from genuine awareness of accountability before Allah (1+1 mark). The concept of stewardship (khalifa on earth) linked to Akhirah encourages environmental responsibility because humans will be accountable for how they treated Allah's creation (1+1 mark). Belief in Barzakh means Muslims regard death not as an end but as a transition, which can bring comfort in grief and reduce the fear of death (1+1 mark). [6 marks: 3 marks per way — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'Descriptions of heaven and hell in Islam should be interpreted literally, not metaphorically.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Qur'an describes al-Jannah and Jahannam in concrete, specific terms — gardens, rivers, fire — suggesting literal reality; many classical scholars and traditional Muslim communities take these descriptions at face value; treating them as metaphor might undermine their moral force and the seriousness of divine reward and punishment; Surah 101 describes cosmic events in graphic language, implying physical reality. Arguments against: Allah is beyond human comprehension, so descriptions of the unseen (ghayb) must necessarily use human language as an approximation; Sufi and philosophical traditions have long read these as metaphors for spiritual states of closeness to or distance from Allah; the Qur'an itself uses simile and parable throughout, suggesting not all imagery is literal; both interpretations are found within mainstream scholarship, suggesting neither is definitively required. Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Surah 101, Surah 2:155, Surah 17:49-51), reference to Sufi or philosophical vs traditional perspectives, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with sourcing; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or limited sourcing. Emerging: Brief, unsupported. [15 marks: SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: State what Muslim theology teaches about the fate of a martyr (shahid) after death.
practice_questions.marks: A martyr is believed to bypass Barzakh and enter paradise (al-Jannah) immediately. [1 mark]

before.exam_tip_html: The predestination topic (al-Qadr) is one of the most nuanced in this unit. Examiners reward students who go beyond simply saying “Muslims believe in fate” and instead explain the Mu’tazilite vs Al-Ash’ari debate, or the tension between divine foreknowledge and human freedom. For Barzakh, make sure you can distinguish it clearly from both death itself and from the final afterlife state — it is the ‘in between.’ For a 15-mark Discuss question on life after death, argue both that literal interpretations reinforce moral seriousness and that metaphorical interpretations may better capture the ineffable nature of the divine. Cite Surah 2:155 (testing), Surah 33:38 (destiny), Surah 101 (Day of Judgement). SPaG marks reward correct spelling: ‘al-Qadr’, ‘Akhirah’, ‘Barzakh’, ‘Jahannam’, ‘Mu’tazilite’.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'pancha sila' in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: The Five Precepts — the basic ethical code for lay Buddhists (accept any equivalent wording that identifies pancha sila as five ethical guidelines). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between the Arahant and the Bodhisattva ideals in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: The Arahant is the Theravada ideal: a fully liberated individual who has eliminated the three poisons and will not be reborn. The Bodhisattva is the Mahayana ideal: a being who seeks Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings, motivated by compassion, delaying final liberation. 1 mark: identifying one ideal correctly. 2 marks: describing both with the key distinction (individual vs universal liberation). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline how kamma shapes a Buddhist's understanding of rebirth.
practice_questions.marks:
Creditworthy points (any 3):
• Kamma is the law of intentional action and consequence: every deliberate action generates kamma.
• Unskilful actions (rooted in the three poisons) generate negative kamma; skilful actions generate positive kamma.
• The result of accumulated kamma is punabbhava — rebirth or rebecoming in a new existence.
• The cycle of rebirth (samsara) continues until the three poisons are extinguished through following the Eightfold Path.
[3 marks, 1 per valid point with brief explanation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the significance of the five khandas for the Buddhist understanding of the self.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The five khandas (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness) are what constitute a 'person'; none is a permanent self.
• Theravada Buddhism uses the khandas to support anatta (no fixed self): each aggregate is impermanent (anicca) and subject to suffering (dukkha), so none can constitute a permanent 'I'.
• The Heart Sutta (Mahayana) extends this via sunyata: 'form is emptiness, emptiness is form' — all five aggregates lack inherent existence.
• The Diamond Sutta reinforces that no fixed characteristics belong to any phenomenon, including the person.
• The practical significance: if the person is not a fixed self, then the clinging to a permanent 'I' (the root of tanha) can be recognised as based on a delusion, making liberation logically possible.
• Mahayana adds tathagatagarbha: within these shifting aggregates is the potential for Buddhahood, balancing emptiness with a positive capacity for Enlightenment.
Mastering: all five khandas listed with their significance for anatta, Theravada and Mahayana treated distinctly, named sources used, significance explained.
Secure: the khandas and their link to anatta explained with at least one named source.
Developing: basic description of the khandas with limited explanation of their significance.
Emerging: a simple mention of the khandas without connecting them to anatta or the self. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The Bodhisattva ideal is more important for Buddhists today than the Arahant ideal.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Bodhisattva ideal, expressed in Santideva's Bodhicaryavatara (3:6–20), combines personal spiritual practice with universal compassion, making it highly relevant to the social and ethical concerns of modern life.
• In a globalised, interconnected world, the Bodhisattva vow to work for the liberation of all beings resonates with contemporary values of social justice and environmental care.
• The Mahayana tradition is numerically dominant worldwide (East Asia, Tibet); for the majority of Buddhists, the Bodhisattva ideal is the living norm of practice.
• Pure Land Buddhism (an extremely popular Mahayana school) makes the Bodhisattva path accessible to ordinary lay people through trust in Amida Buddha's compassionate vow.

Arguments against or offering a different emphasis:
• The Arahant ideal remains the living standard in Theravada countries (Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand), which have large and vibrant Buddhist populations. Claiming the Bodhisattva ideal is 'more important' overlooks the lived reality of Theravada communities.
• The Arahant ideal emphasises personal discipline, meditation and inner transformation — these are timeless and do not depend on cultural context. Many argue that if each individual achieved liberation, the collective benefit would be the same.
• Both ideals share the same basis: the Eightfold Path, the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths. The distinction between Arahant and Bodhisattva is one of emphasis and scope, not fundamental doctrine.
• The Karaniya Metta Sutta, a Theravada text, already teaches universal loving kindness (metta) to all beings — suggesting that the Theravada tradition also contains the compassionate motivation associated with the Bodhisattva ideal.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Santideva's Bodhicaryavatara 3:6–20, Karaniya Metta Sutta), Theravada/Mahayana distinction accurately maintained, explicit weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered with at least one named source and a clear conclusion.
Developing: some argument on each side with limited sources.
Emerging: one-sided or superficial response with no sources. [15 marks, SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning and importance of metta (loving kindness) in Buddhist ethics.
practice_questions.marks:
Creditworthy points (any 3 from the following):
• Metta means loving kindness or benevolence — the wish for all beings to be happy without exception.
• The Karaniya Metta Sutta teaches the practice of metta as a meditation, cultivating goodwill toward all sentient beings including enemies.
• Metta is one of the four brahmaviharas (divine abodes), alongside karuna (compassion), mudita (sympathetic joy) and upekkha (equanimity); it is central to Buddhist ethics because it generates the positive motivation that underpins all skilful action.
[3 marks, 1 per valid point with brief explanation]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'sanatana dharma'.
practice_questions.marks: The eternal dharma; the name many Hindus use for their religion, indicating that its truths are ancient, universal and timeless. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Hindu virtue of ahimsa.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: ahimsa means non-violence or harmlessness; it requires not causing harm in thought, word or action to any living being; it is described as the highest dharma in the Mahabharata (V 39); Gandhi applied it in campaigns for independence; it is one of the central yamas (moral restraints). [2 marks — 1 for a simple statement, 2 for a developed description]

practice_questions.text: Outline the four Purusharthas (aims of human life) in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: the four Purusharthas are dharma (duty/righteousness), artha (material prosperity), kama (pleasure/desire) and moksha (liberation); dharma acts as the regulating principle for artha and kama; moksha is the highest aim; together they present a holistic vision of human flourishing; the Bhagavad Gita (VIII 8-12) points towards moksha as the ultimate horizon. [3 marks — 1 for naming two or more Purusharthas, 2 for briefly describing them, 3 for a full outline explaining dharma's regulating role and moksha as the highest aim]

practice_questions.text: Explain two different Hindu views on the importance of varna (social division) in living according to dharma.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Traditional view: varna reflects the cosmic order established by Brahman; each social class has specific dharmic duties described in the Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1-3); performing one's varna duty is a form of worship and keeps the social and cosmic order in harmony.
• Reform view: the hereditary caste system has been used to oppress Dalits, which contradicts the spirit of dharma as righteous conduct; the Mahabharata (V 39) golden rule ('do not do to others what you would not wish done to yourself') implies equality; thinkers such as Ambedkar challenged caste hierarchy as a corruption of genuine dharma.
[6 marks — 3 marks per view: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a developed explanation with a source or named position]

practice_questions.text: 'The concept of dharma is the most important Hindu teaching.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments that could support the statement: dharma is described as the regulating principle that frames all other aims of life (Purusharthas); sanatana dharma is the name Hindus give to their entire religious tradition; the yamas (ahimsa, daya, dama, dana) all express dharma in practical terms; the Bhagavad Gita (II 31) teaches that one’s own dharma is irreplaceable; the Mahabharata (V 39) places ahimsa — an expression of dharma — at the centre of ethical life; without dharma, the pursuit of artha and kama becomes selfish and harmful.

Arguments that could challenge the statement: moksha (liberation) could be seen as more important because it is the ultimate goal that gives all other aims their meaning; the teaching on karma and samsara is arguably the foundation from which dharma draws its urgency; understanding Brahman (Saguna/Nirguna) is the deepest theological teaching; bhakti (loving devotion) traditions might argue that love of God is more central than duty; the concept of atman (the eternal self) is arguably prior to dharma since it explains why moral choices matter at all.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita II 31, XVI 1-3, VIII 8-12; Mahabharata V 39), explicit weighing of arguments, and a justified conclusion that takes a clear position.
Secure: two clear perspectives with some use of Hindu teaching; conclusion present.
Developing: one side more developed; some relevant content; limited source use.
Emerging: one-sided or very brief; little specific Hindu content.

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning and importance of the yamas in Hindu ethical life.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: yamas are moral restraints or virtues that apply to all human beings regardless of varna or ashrama; they include ahimsa (non-violence), daya (compassion), dama (self-control) and dana (generosity); the Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1-3) describes qualities of a 'divine nature' that correspond to the yamas; they express dharma in everyday relationships; ahimsa is described as the highest dharma in the Mahabharata (V 39). [3 marks — 1 for identifying the yamas as moral virtues, 2 for explaining one or two with specific content, 3 for a full outline naming multiple yamas with their meaning and textual grounding]
